Overview

General wisdom states that goats were the first animals to be successfully domesticated. Goats are associated with love, knowledge, fertility, prophesy, expiation, regeneration, and rebirth. They are intensely associated with sex, sexual energy, and the procreative urge and power.

Goats and Discovery

Goats are involved in a lot of firsts. Goats are credited with leading people to coffee, once a sacred beverage. An Ethiopian shepherd noticed that his goats were particularly perky; he watched as they chewed coffee berries and tried some himself, thus initiating the cult of caffeine. Goats brought various fragrant resins to people, most especially rock roses, among Aphrodite's holy flowers. The aromatic essence was discovered clinging to goats' beards.

Ancient Spiritual Evidence

Some of the most ancient existing evidence of magickal and spiritual ritual involves the unearthed funeral rites of a Neanderthal child discovered in Teshik-Tash, modern Uzbekistan. The child's partial skeleton was encircled by ibex horns, a type of wild goat, arranged vertically in pairs, the pointed ends stuck into the ground, reminiscent of later European funerary spells that involve driving spindles into the ground, usually intended to quiet the restless dead.

The Oracle of Delphi

Goats are responsible for the discovery of the Oracle of Delphi. Before there was ever a shrine, Delphi was a playground for goats, which thrived on the rocky terrain. Humans followed them up the slopes and domesticated them c. 1400 BCE. As legend tells it, a massive earthquake created a chasm or fissure at Delphi through which some sort of vapor emanated. Goats exposed to the vapors were observed to act strangely, suffering spasms and bleating in odd voices. Their keepers began to have similar experiences except that their odd voices were discovered to be prophetic. Delphi eventually became an organized oracular shrine, originally dedicated to Gaia, the Earth and then to Apollo. Goats remained the ritual sacrifice at Delphi.

Sacred Companions and Mounts

Goats serve as Aphrodite's mount and as companions of various Middle Eastern fertility spirits, including Inanna-Ishtar and Lady Asherah. Perceptions change: once upon a time, comparing a man to a goat implied admiration. Today's "old goat" is a pathetic, foolish lecher, kind of like those dumb-ass donkeys.

Ancient Spiritual Traditions

Goats were profoundly involved with a multitude of ancient spiritual traditions including Celtic, Greek, Jewish, Norse, Roman, and Sumerian. Goats are sacred to Aphrodite, Azazel, Dionysus, Freyja, Hera, Hermes, Thor, Zeus: sexy deities, one and all. Goats were respected, sacred, and beloved in ancient religion. Goats were people's teachers, companions and in many places, primary food animal, supplying meat, milk, dairy products, and material for clothing and tents.

Witches and Goats

Goats were not generally considered to be witches' familiars, nor do witches transform into goats. Goats do frequently serve as witches' mounts however, and many medieval woodblock prints depicting witchcraft show witches riding on goats' backs, just like Aphrodite, although this may have been intended to euphemistically suggest that witches copulate with the devil.

Symbolism

More than anything the goat is infamous as an emblem of lust and procreation. Much of that reputation traces to the so-called Goat of Mendes, sometimes called Baphomet, of ancient Egypt, a powerful deity honored through rites that celebrated the procreative force of nature. The Greeks identified this god with Pan, the god of nature, who sometimes wore goatskins.

The Romans likewise saw the goat as a creature of lasciviousness and fertility. Barren women were counseled to couple with goats, or to have their backs lashed with strips cut from the hide of a sacrificed goat, a rite thought to purify them. This may have lent its name to the festival of Lupercalia, possibly from a phrase meaning to purify by means of the goat. The animal's shaggy hair and horns added to its reputation for sexual vigor, and it was said that a single male could service a hundred and fifty females. The goat and human hybrid known as the Satyr was imagined as the product of such carnality, a warning of what becomes of those who surrender to base desire.

In some traditions the goat is a creature of fire, and in particular the fire of lightning. In the Vedic tales of India, Agni, lord of fire, rides upon a goat. China and Tibet held a similar image, casting the goat as a messenger that carries the blessings of the gods in their heavens down to people on earth. The ancient Greeks made the she-goat a sign of lightning, immortalizing the goat that suckled the infant Zeus on sacred Mount Ida as the constellation Amalthea. When that constellation was visible, storms and rain were expected, and language preserves the connection, for the word aegis names both a goatskin and stormy weather.

Then there is the scapegoat, first described in the Old Testament. A rite used two goats, one set free and one sacrificed. The freed goat was burdened with the sins of the people and driven into the desert to perish, its end often hastened by being cast from a cliff. The name of that cliff, Azazel, meaning the goat that departs, was also the name of a demon. The idea survives today, the scapegoat being one who carries the blame for the wrongs of others, and it has at times cast the goat as a figure of the unrepentant sinner.

The Devil as Goat

No animal is more associated with the Christian devil than the goat. Artistic renditions of the sabbat from the Middle Ages to Goya's masterpieces depict Satan presiding over the witches' sabbat in the form of a tall man-sized upright goat. Satan is also depicted as a composite creature, frequently with bat's wings and a snake's forked tongue, but with goat's eyes, horns and hooves.

The hawk is a sharp-eyed, fierce, and highly intelligent bird of prey found on nearly every continent, carrying associations with solar power, nobility, divine messengership, and the capacity to see what others miss. One of the most widely recognized raptors in human mythology and magickal practice, it calls us to sharpen our perception and reconnect with the wilder aspects of ourselves.

Physical Description

Hawks are small to medium-sized diurnal birds of prey with sharp, hooked beaks built for tearing. Their plumage is generally brown or grey with lighter barring on the wings and back. The red-tailed hawk, the most common hawk in North America, measures approximately 22 inches in length with a 48-inch wingspan and weighs around 3 pounds. As with many raptors, the female is typically larger than the male.

Habitat and Distribution

Hawks are found worldwide except in Antarctica. They occupy an unusually broad range of environments: mountains, coastal regions, grasslands, woodlands, and agricultural areas alike. Their adaptability makes them one of the most commonly encountered birds of prey across nearly all landscapes.

Behavior

The hawk is a highly intelligent hunter, historically prized and trained for falconry. Its exceptional eyesight allows it to spot prey from great distances while soaring. In many traditions, falcons and hawks are effectively interchangeable in both mythology and magickal symbolism. A group of hawks is collectively called a cast or a kettle.

Mythology and Folklore

The hawk is recognized across cultures for its powerful wings, piercing vision, and ferocious nature. Its long history as a hunting companion associated it firmly with nobility and aristocracy. In Greek mythology, a hawk served as the messenger of Apollo, the god of the sun, prophecy, music, and healing, deepening the hawk's solar and oracular associations.

Omens and Divinatory Meaning

The hawk is a call back to the wild self. If you have become too enmeshed in artificial environments or disconnected from the more instinctual, untamed parts of your nature, the hawk urges a return: a walk in nature, time away from screens, contact with the living world. Balance cannot be maintained without it.

Like the falcon and eagle, the hawk also signals that something close at hand requires sharper attention. You may have missed something on a first pass. Step back and look at the whole picture rather than a single detail. The hawk can also carry a message about vision in the broader sense, encouraging you to think further ahead and with greater clarity, to consider yourself not just a participant in circumstances but a potential architect of them.

Colors

Grey, brown, beige

Feather Magick

Use hawk feathers in charms and spells for protection.

A Brief Introduction to Astrology

Astrology views humanity as shaped not only by genetics and environment, but also by the configuration of the solar system at the moment of birth. The Sun, Moon, and planets act as fundamental life forces, both the substance we are made of and the tools we live by. Their influence shifts according to their zodiacal position and the angles they form with one another.

A Long Lineage

Astrology is among the oldest surviving occult sciences. Sophisticated systems flourished in Babylonian, Egyptian, and Aztec cultures, with substantial records surviving from each. For centuries in the West, astrology was a respected method of divination, supported and consulted by royal courts. The rise of empirical science in the seventeenth century pushed it toward the realm of superstition, but it never lost its following entirely. Today it remains widely practiced across every walk of life.

The Horoscope

Popular astrology centers on the horoscope, a chart mapping the positions of the planets, the Sun, the Moon, and the stars at the moment of a person's birth. Reading that chart interprets how those celestial placements bear on human affairs.

The Sun passes through the twelve signs of the zodiac across the year. Someone said to be born under Pisces was born during the Sun's transit through the zone of the zodiac named for the constellation Pisces. Each of the twelve signs carries its own personality traits, and the element tied to a sign's ruling planet (fire, water, earth, or air) shapes how that Sun sign expresses itself. The daily positions of the other planets layer further influence on top.

Decanates

As the Sun moves through a single zodiac sign over the course of a month, it crosses three decanates, each about ten days long. Every decanate adds the influence of an additional planet and sign on top of the basic Sun-sign reading, refining the interpretation for an individual birthday.

An Aries born in the third decanate (April 10 to 21), for example, picks up the influence of Sagittarius, the third decanate sign, and its ruling planet Jupiter. The ancient Egyptians considered decanates as important as the Sun signs themselves.

Progressions

Progressions are another widely used predictive technique. With this method, the Sun is treated as moving about thirty years through each sign of the zodiac. Over an average lifespan a person's progressed Sun typically travels through three or four signs. Each shift from one sign to the next marks a turning point, often coinciding with a significant change in circumstance or outlook.

A Scorpio born on November 9, for instance, has a progressed Sun that moves into Sagittarius around age thirteen, into Capricorn around age forty-three, and into Aquarius around age seventy-three.

Fixed Stars

Specific fixed stars tied to particular days of the year exert further influence on a birthday reading. Decanates, progressions, and fixed stars can sound intimidating, but the calculations are usually folded into pre-built birthday profiles, so the reader simply consults the result.

What the Research Suggests

Skeptics argue that the link between planetary position and human destiny is unproven. Recent research on the season, and even the month, of birth complicates that dismissal.

In the early 1970s, a study compiled from the British population census found that architects tended to be born in spring, secretaries in summer, miners in fall, and electricians in winter. The same researcher asked astrologers to predict which signs would dominate two professions, nurses and labor union officials, then ran a large survey to test the prediction. Nurses skewed toward Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, and Pisces, while labor union officials clustered under the remaining signs, matching the astrologers' calls.

Other work has focused on the Sun itself. Ultraviolet radiation is thought to cause genetic changes in the developing foetus that may shape later life and personality, which would help explain why people born around the same time of year often share traits and trajectories.

Analysis of European birth records has found that month of birth measurably affects lifespan. The chance of living past one hundred ran up to 16 percent higher than average for those born in December, and 23 percent lower for those born in June. A separate study reached a similar conclusion, with December births living roughly three years longer on average.

One leading hypothesis is that December babies were conceived in March, possibly avoiding the most damaging solar radiation peaks early in pregnancy. By this argument, the radiation experienced at conception can influence personality and health for decades, which would make where someone is born at least as important as when.

Selected Findings

Happiness. People born in June, July, and August tend to be happier on average. People born in December, January, and February tend to be more pessimistic.

Personality. A study of two thousand people found that women born between February and April were more likely to be novelty seekers than those born in October. Men born in spring tended to be more impulsive, while those born in winter were more inclined to introspection.

Intelligence. A long-term study of twenty-one thousand children found seasonal variations in intelligence, weight, height, and head size. Winter-born children tended to be larger and more academically inclined than summer-born children. A separate study, however, found female students born in spring and summer achieved better exam marks than those born in fall and winter.

Health. Women born in fall reported the fewest menopausal symptoms, while those born in spring reported the most. Winter births carry a greater risk of heart disease, and other work has linked winter birth to a higher risk of obesity.

The Planets

Since the earliest times people have held that the planets of the solar system press a steady, unrelenting influence upon the affairs of the world and of each person within it. What sets a planet apart from a star is its motion, for a planet travels in an orbit around a star; the word itself comes from the Greek planaomai, meaning wanderer.

By tradition there were seven planets, a count that fell into neat agreement with the seven days of the week, the visible colors of the rainbow, the seven magickal metals, the seven heavens, the seven stages of the alchemical Great Work, and the Seven Deadly Sins. Each planet carries the name of a god, and the clearest sign of their influence is read in the zodiac. In the Kabbalah the planets are named as spheres, and they too fall under the care of angels.

The very building of the musical scale is owed to the planets. Legend tells that the Muses brought music into being by listening to the note each of the seven planets sang as it turned in its celestial orbit, and the harmonies they made together were believed to hold the cosmos itself in being.

Life Under the Moon

This guide explores the deep, ancient relationship between the moon and all life on Earth. From her role in shaping the planet's tides and seasons to her influence on animals, plants, and human behavior, the moon has been a guiding force since the earliest days of existence. Understanding these connections strengthens your awareness of lunar energy and how it weaves through every layer of your magickal practice.

The Moon and Earth

The moon likely formed at least 4.5 billion years ago when a massive celestial body collided with young Earth. Scientists named the impactor Theia, after the titan mother of Selene, the Greek goddess of the moon. The collision sent enough debris into space to coalesce and eventually form the moon. Analysis of basaltic rock samples has confirmed the shared composition of the Earth and moon, showing that the moon was born in part from the Earth itself.

At the time of her formation, the moon was much closer to us. Even now, she drifts roughly 1.5 inches farther from the Earth each year. Without her presence, life here would be profoundly different. The gravitational exchange between the two bodies has steadied the seasons, lengthened our days, and created the tides that shaped the world as we know it.

The moon takes approximately 27.3 days to complete one orbit around the Earth. However, because the Earth is also moving during that time, the moon must travel a bit farther to realign with the sun, resulting in a full lunar cycle of about 29.5 days from one new moon to the next. Her orbit is elliptical rather than perfectly circular, tracing a slightly elongated path.

Lunar Tides

Although the moon's gravity is far weaker than the Earth's, its effects are significant. As the moon orbits, her gravitational pull displaces ocean water, creating high tides on the sides of the Earth closest to and farthest from the moon. The water drawn toward these points is displaced from elsewhere, producing low tides at the points roughly 90 degrees out from the highs.

When the Earth, sun, and moon align during the new moon and full moon, their combined gravitational forces create especially dramatic tidal shifts known as spring tides. About seven days later, when the moon and sun form a right angle (coinciding with the first and last quarter moons), the sun's gravitational pull partially offsets the moon's, producing gentler changes called neap tides.

Billions of years ago, when the moon was closer and the Earth spun more rapidly, these tides would have been far more extreme. The churning of ancient coastlines stirred essential minerals into the water, and some scientists believe this process played a critical role in the evolution of life on Earth.

Seasons and the Length of Day

The moon's gravitational relationship with the Earth influences more than just the tides. The Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5 degrees, and as different hemispheres point toward or away from the sun throughout the year, we experience the changing seasons. Without the moon, these seasons could become far more extreme, because the Earth's tilt is not perfectly fixed. It has a slight wobble, and the moon's gravity helps stabilize it, keeping the seasons relatively consistent.

Over immense stretches of time, the moon's gravitational pull has also slowed the Earth's rotation, gradually lengthening our days. Fossil evidence shows that the Earth once had much shorter days than the 24-hour cycle we know today.

Sea Creatures and the Lunar Cycle

Marine life offers some of the most visible examples of lunar influence. The tides created by the moon shape the life cycles of countless ocean creatures. Nesting and newborn sea turtles rely on moonlight to navigate shorelines safely at night, when temperatures are cooler and predators are fewer. Oysters and other shellfish open and close in rhythm with the moon's phases and the resulting ocean currents. The moon's light and its pull on the water also guide marine creatures in their patterns of mating, birthing, feeding, and migration.

Animals and the Moon

The moon's influence extends well beyond the ocean. Ecologists studying the behavior of prey animals in relation to the lunar cycle observed that wildebeest adjusted their activity based on moon phases, staying in sheltered, safer areas during the dark moon. During the full moon, they ventured into more open territory where encounters with predators like lions were more likely, because the increased visibility allowed them to spot threats at a distance. Predators with strong night vision, on the other hand, may have an advantage under the dark moon, when shadows conceal their approach.

Birds adjust feeding and migration patterns according to the lunar cycle, and even dung beetles navigate by moonlight as they roll their cargo away from competitors and predators.

Plants and the Moon

Plant life is attuned to the moon as well. A Mediterranean plant called the joint pine produces droplets of fluid that refract moonlight, creating tiny sparkles that attract nocturnal pollinators. Many night-flowering plants depend on moonlight to draw moths and other nighttime visitors, a process essential to their reproduction and survival.

Lunar gardening is a longstanding practice in many traditions. Some practitioners maintain that the waxing-to-full moon increases the movement of sap within plants, while the waning moon slows it down, making certain phases better for planting, pruning, and harvesting.

Moonlight and Human Behavior

Humans are also attuned to the moon, even in an age of artificial lighting and digital screens. Many people who work in hospitals and emergency services report an increase in incidents during the full moon, though formal research remains inconclusive. At a minimum, the moon may influence sleep patterns by affecting levels of melatonin, the hormone that regulates the sleep-wake cycle. The emerging study of human circalunar rhythms, the body's response to the 29.5-day lunar cycle, may eventually reveal much more about how deeply the moon's presence is woven into our biology.

The Moon in Human History

Since the earliest days of human life, the moon, sun, and sky have shaped daily existence. Early humans tracked the moon's passage across the sky to measure time, and folklore about the moon persists to this day, from reading a ring around the moon as a sign of coming rain to planting and harvesting crops by her phases. The lunar cycle's correspondence with the seasons (three to four lunations per season) helped our ancestors anticipate and prepare for each turning of the year.

Early Lunar Timekeeping

The question of when humans first began tracking the moon remains a subject of ongoing research. Cave paintings of animals and the night sky, such as those found in the Lascaux caves in France, demonstrate early creativity and may reflect the moon's power to inspire. These images may also have served ritualistic and spiritual purposes, calling for blessings and luck in hunts, possibly making them some of the earliest recorded lunar rites. Research published in 2023 found that notations of lines, dots, and Y-shaped marks in certain cave paintings corresponded with animal activity and the lunar cycle, suggesting that humans may have been actively timekeeping with the moon as far back as 37,000 to 42,000 years ago.

Beyond timekeeping, the moon would have aided nighttime hunting, foraging, and travel, casting a luminous glow across the landscape. Our ancestors lived by the rhythms of the moon, the sun, and the seasons, and it was only natural for the moon to be personified as a deity.

The Moon as a Deity

With the agricultural revolution and the development of writing, records of specific moon deities emerged, connecting the moon to timekeeping and the fertility of life. To countless ancient cultures, celestial bodies were gods, and the moon was among the most revered.

In ancient Sumeria, the moon god Nanna (also known as Sin) was one of the most prominent deities. Nanna was depicted as an old man or cowherd and was closely associated with the bull and the cow, both ancient fertility symbols. Through his family, Nanna was connected to fertility, abundance, and the realm of the dead.

The phases of the moon held deep significance and guided the timing of rituals and rites. The Egyptian moon deity Khonsu, whose name means "traveler," was a god of healing, fertility, and time. He was often petitioned at the appearance of the waxing crescent for blessings of fertility for both people and animals.

Even as permanent settlements led many cultures toward sun-centered worship, the moon remained vital. Without electricity, moonlight was essential for nighttime travel. Seafaring demanded knowledge of the moon, tides, and stars. Agricultural communities relied on lunar cycles for the fertility of crops, livestock, and people alike.

Suppression and Survival

As Christianity spread and the church's influence grew in Western culture, nature-based deities, including moon gods, were suppressed in favor of a single deity. Leaders discouraged people from accessing the healing power of nature and the moon. Worship of lunar deities went underground, and healers lived on the margins of society, quietly continuing to use the moon for gardening, harvesting, travel, and healing.

The Moon in Religious Traditions Today

The moon continues to guide religious observance around the world. Ramadan spans from crescent moon to crescent moon. Easter falls on the Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox. Many Jewish holidays are marked by the full moon. In China, the lunar new year is a cornerstone of cultural life, and the Mid-Autumn Moon Festival honors the lunar goddess Chang'e, who drank an elixir of immortality and ascended to the moon. Harvest moon festivals, both sacred and secular, are still celebrated across many traditions.

The moon landing may have stripped away some of her mystery, but it also deepened our connection to her. India and China have both named spacecraft after their lunar deities. The moon's light continues to inspire, and she is experiencing a revival of reverence as modern witches weave her energy into their practice.

The Moon and Witchcraft Today

The moon has been intertwined with spells and rituals for as long as magick has been practiced. While the forms may have shifted over the centuries, witches today still follow her call.

How the Moon Aids Witches

Modern witches connect with the moon in countless ways:

  • Manifesting desires by casting intentions at the new and full moons
  • Hosting lunar gatherings and coven rituals under the full moon
  • Meditating to align with lunar energy
  • Charging water under the moon for use in spellcrafting
  • Letting the moon's phases guide when to cast, heal, and reflect
  • Charging crystals and conducting healing rituals by the light of the full moon
  • Planting, nurturing, and harvesting healing herbs according to the moon's phases
  • Using the 29.5-day lunar cycle from new moon to new moon to build habits, set monthly goals, and work toward long-term intentions
  • Drawing on the moon's phase, sign, and seasonality to guide reflection and focus

At its core, working with the moon allows witches to access a deeper layer of magickal power and healing. The moon is both part of us and a source of energy for spellwork. Some practitioners are so closely attuned to her that their own energy and psychic sensitivity rise and fall with her cycle.

Embracing Dark and Light

The moon's cycle reflects the polarity of dark and light that is central to witchcraft: the unknown and the known, the spiritual realm and waking reality, the subconscious and the conscious. Like the dark moon goddess Hekate, who holds the keys to secrets and mysteries, moon witches are unafraid to explore the shadows and find power in the dark. There is a cycle and a season for everything under the moon. Her phases offer a time for rest and retreat, a time for growth and change, and a time to stand fully in your power.

The Moon in Western Astrology

In Western astrology, the moon is considered feminine and represents the soul, the subconscious, early childhood, and patterns of nurturing. Her cycles often draw what is hidden in the subconscious into conscious awareness. In modern times, the moon has taken on a particularly significant role in the reawakening of goddess energy, calling practitioners to honor the power of the feminine.

An Enduring Symbol

The moon is our relative, born of Earth and stardust, just as we are. She has watched over our ancestors and will continue to watch over future generations, a steady light in the sky connecting everyone to the past, present, and future. Just as harvest moon gratitude rituals have been observed for generations, the moon can serve as a bridge to ancestors and spirits beyond the veil. Through her patient, nurturing presence, all things can come to manifest.

Working with Stones in Spellcraft

Stones do not have to be faceted or expensive. They do not even have to be tumbled smooth, large, or of the best quality. Some stones are multi-functional, so you don't need a different one for each spell unless you are trying to do more than one spell at a time, which isn't advised. Handle several stones of a kind to see which feels right to you. You can keep them in a plastic bag with a label until you can differentiate between the types.

Most stones can, and should, be rinsed in water to cleanse them of all vibrations except yours. One exception is calcite, which is too soft to endure water. Cleanse calcite by surrounding it with quartz crystals for twenty-four hours.

When your spell is completed and you empty the used herbs on the ground, pick up and cleanse the used stones again. Stones shouldn't be wasted; they are not an infinite resource.

Stones make charm bags and poppets more powerful. You can go only by the color of the stones if you wish, but more energy is drawn to your project if certain stones are used. The planetary list on each planet's page will help you decide on the weekday — and hour of the day — to further fine-tune your working.

In magickal and astrological tradition, the luminaries (sun and moon) are classified as planets alongside other heavenly bodies, despite differing from modern astronomical definitions. Both astrology and magick operate as geocentric systems, perceiving everything as revolving around Earth even when this is not literally the case.

Every day, hour, topic, and category carries a planetary correspondence. This applies across Western, Chinese, and Hindu magickal systems, though their respective astrological frameworks differ. The Western system derives from Babylonian astrology, which heavily influenced Egyptian and Greek traditions.

Every planet possesses astrological and magickal influence (ancient Greek and Roman curse tablets fell under the dominion of Saturn, for instance), but the planets most strongly identified with magick are Earth and the Moon.

Earth

Where the Moon represents psychic ability, Earth represents general vitality. Both are required for optimal magick power. According to many worldwide traditions, Earth is the material from which humans are created. Earth is our mother: we are born from her body and returned to her to await rebirth while the corporeal body decays and becomes part of Earth once more, in a never-ending cycle. Without extended, consistent physical contact with Earth, vitality and magick power suffer and diminish.

Earth is also very literally the dirt underfoot. Dirt empowers both practitioners and spells. Various traditions pursue physical healing by packing patients into heated sand. Moor mud detoxifies the body. Dirt from shrines and saints' tombs is perceived as exceptionally charged with power. Bits of dirt are carried as talismans and sprinkled over items to empower and revitalize them.

The most famous magickal dirt comes from the Roman Catholic shrine at Chimayo, New Mexico, though the dirt's miraculous reputation predates Catholicism in the area. Thousands converge on Chimayo annually for its healing properties.

Certain magickal traditions rely on the power of dirt more than others. The Afro-Caribbean tradition of Palo Monte utilizes more types of dirt than perhaps any other, with spells requesting specific amounts of dirt from locations like police stations, courthouses, and hospitals. This magickal tradition dates back at least to ancient Mesopotamia.

Most traditions utilize certain specific types of magickal dirt, including:

  • Crossroads dirt
  • Footprint dirt
  • Graveyard dirt

Inherent energy is transmitted through contact with the dirt itself.

The Moon

The Moon is considered the ruler of all magickal arts, and magick is timed to the phases of the Moon:

  • Waxing Moon: Spells intended to increase something (like money) or initiate something new (a fresh romance) are coordinated with the waxing moon. Begin these spells on or just after the New Moon.
  • Waning Moon: Spells intended to decrease something (like debt) or cast for the purpose of banishing are coordinated with the waning moon. Begin these spells on or just after the Full Moon.
  • Dark of the Moon: The few days where the Moon is not visible, just prior to the rebirth of the New Moon, are controversial. Some traditions avoid casting spells during this period. Others, particularly those devoted to Dark Moon spirits like Hecate or Lilith, consider this a period of profound magickal power.

In Arabic folk custom, whatever you find yourself doing at the moment you first glimpse the brand new Moon is considered the right thing for you to do.

Exposing magickal tools, charms, and preparations to the beams of the Full Moon provides enhanced magickal empowerment, though this does not eliminate the need to charge items with personal energy.

Magick worked directly with the Moon (rather than simply timing by phase) is traditionally women's magick. A trinity exists between the Moon, women, the ocean, and by implication all water. The Moon profoundly affects menstrual cycles and the tides. Since women have a natural affinity for the Moon, they may more readily draw on its power.

Most lunar deities are female, including Artemis, Diana, Hecate, Selene, Lady Chang'o, and Ix Chel. In ancient Egypt, however, the Moon was perceived as male precisely because of its demonstrated influence over women's fertility.

Drawing Down the Moon

This term refers to specific Wiccan spiritual rites in which the Goddess is invited to enter the body of her priestess and speak through her. Some traditions also practice a parallel Drawing Down the Sun ritual, invoking male divine energy. However, Drawing Down the Moon is a very ancient term predating modern Wicca that may refer to various rites depending on the magickal tradition, most especially the process of creating moon-infused waters.

Charm Bags & Poppets

Choose the herbs and stones that you feel good about using and are within your budget. The power of your intent will be what makes them all work together to fulfill your wish.

Charm bags and poppets don't have to be very large. In fact, small is often better. You can pin a small charm bag to the inside of your bra or carry it easily in your pocket. A poppet can fit just as easily into a drawer — that way no one sees it and thinks you are up to some negative mischief. Fill most of the poppet or charm bag with cotton balls or quilt batting; you will be putting a lot of your intent energy into the spoonful of herbs you add.

Poppets

The poppet is primarily used for healing on yourself or others. You can draw on facial features. Poppets are stuffed with appropriate herbs and a stone (or stones) placed inside where the illness is. The poppet requires two cut pieces of muslin or fabric — sew up the sides first and leave a small opening to stuff in the herbs and stones, then finish sewing the poppet shut.

Charm Bags

Sew three sides shut, stuff in the herbs and stones, then sew the packet closed. You can also use fabric glue instead of sewing. The charm bag needs only one piece of fabric cut — it will be bent in half, the two sides sewed or glued together, and then the top closed after the herbs are inside.

You can choose different herbs and stones than those suggested, and you can change any chant or make up your own. The most important part is to be clear in your intent and concentrate on it very hard while holding the finished poppet or charm bag.

The ancient Greeks called this technique "drawing down the moon" or the "Thessalian Trick." Thessalian witches were believed to hold great power and metaphysical knowledge, and this was considered one of their most important formulas.

Using the Moon Phases in Magick

Once you know the Moon’s phases and the kind of spiritual tone each one carries, you can start applying that rhythm to your practice. You might time a single spell to the phase that best supports it, or work with one intention across the whole lunation through small, phase-matched actions.

Ways to work with the lunar cycle include:

  • Casting spells when the phase naturally supports the outcome
  • Reinforcing a goal through brief meditations in multiple phases
  • Scheduling tarot or oracle readings when insight is easier to access
  • Doing supporting work to keep momentum moving toward a longer-term desire
  • Using the waxing and waning rhythm as a mirror for personal reflection, healing, and manifestation

As you build familiarity, you can also choose to create a different working for each phase, letting the Moon shape the entire month of magick.

Special Lunar Occasions

Beyond the regular cycle, certain lunar alignments add an extra layer of intensity. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up in particular ways, you may experience events like eclipses, supermoons, blue moons, and black moons.

Older cultures often treated these events with awe and anxiety, weaving stories that explained the sudden shift in the sky as omens, warnings, or signs of divine power. Even with modern astronomy clarifying what is happening, these moments can still feel charged and uncanny. In magickal practice, they are often approached as times when change accelerates and themes become harder to ignore.

Eclipses

An eclipse occurs when the alignment of the new or full moon is close enough that either the Moon obscures the Sun (solar eclipse) or Earth’s shadow darkens the Moon (lunar eclipse). Eclipses are commonly framed as energetic shake-ups that can trigger major inner and outer shifts.

Eclipses often arrive in pairs and can create a concentrated stretch of intensity sometimes called eclipse season. Many practitioners find that eclipses highlight life themes connected to the Sun and Moon as symbols: identity, purpose, and the conscious self (Sun) alongside intuition, emotion, and the subconscious (Moon).

Because eclipses occur in specific zodiac signs, they can emphasize different lessons depending on where they land for you. Their influence may echo for months, especially when a later lunation in the same sign completes or clarifies what was set in motion.

Solar Eclipses

Solar eclipses happen when the Moon moves between Earth and the Sun, blocking some or all of the Sun from view. They occur only at the new moon. Although each eclipse is brief, it can coincide with a broader period of shifting energy, and it is often paired with a lunar eclipse near a surrounding full moon.

Because the Moon’s shadow is relatively narrow, any given solar eclipse is only visible from certain parts of the world. Even so, many practitioners treat the energetic tone as collective and noticeable whether or not the eclipse is visible locally.

Types of solar eclipses include:

  • Partial: The Moon covers part of the Sun, leaving a bright crescent visible.
  • Annular: The Moon crosses the Sun when it is farther from Earth, so a ring of sunlight remains visible.
  • Total: The Moon fully covers the Sun for a short span of time.

In magickal terms, solar eclipses are often approached as amplified new-moon portals, closing one chapter while pushing a new direction into motion. They can bring closure, realizations, and decisive pivots, along with a sense of being re-aimed toward a truer path.

If you choose to work with a solar eclipse, focus on intention-setting and practical alignment. Vision boards, guided meditation, crystal healing, sound work, and action planning can help you meet the moment with clarity. Many practitioners also release what is ready to end just before the point of exact alignment, then commit to the new direction as the portal opens.

Lunar Eclipses

A lunar eclipse happens when Earth moves between the Sun and the full Moon, casting its shadow across the lunar surface. From the night side of Earth, the Moon may darken or shift in color, sometimes taking on a deep red tone.

Lunar eclipses involve two layers of Earth’s shadow:

  • Penumbra: the outer shadow
  • Umbra: the darker central shadow

Types of lunar eclipses include:

  • Penumbral: The Moon passes through the penumbra only, creating a subtle dimming or slight change in tone.
  • Partial: Part of the Moon enters the umbra, and the shaded area can appear red, orange, brown, or yellow.
  • Total: The entire Moon moves through the umbra. Because it also crosses the penumbra on the way in and out, this is the longest form of lunar eclipse and can last for a couple of hours.

Magickally, lunar eclipses are often treated as intensified full moons. Emotions can feel amplified, and situations may come to a head quickly. Some practitioners avoid outcome-driven spellwork during these windows because the energy can feel erratic. Others use the potency for major manifestation or for work that requires a decisive turning point.

Because the full moon is already a time of culmination, a lunar eclipse can accelerate endings and reveal what has been hidden. Old wounds, repeating patterns, and unspoken truths may rise to the surface, creating vulnerability alongside a strong opportunity for healing. This is also a potent time to check in with your path: what is reaching completion, what needs to be released, and what kind of transformation is asking to begin.

Many practitioners also find psychic sensitivity heightened during a lunar eclipse. Divination, spirit communication, and reflective ritual can feel especially vivid, provided you stay grounded.

Supermoons and Micromoons

The Moon's orbit around Earth is elliptical, so its distance from us changes throughout each cycle. The closest point is called the perigee, and the farthest is the apogee.

When a full moon lines up at or near perigee, it is known as a supermoon or perigee moon. This happens roughly three to four times per year. A supermoon can appear up to fourteen percent larger and about thirty percent brighter than a micromoon (a full moon at apogee). The stronger gravitational pull at perigee can also produce higher-than-usual tides.

Many practitioners describe supermoon energy as amplified and electric, with heightened emotions and sharper psychic impressions. Manifestation work, lunar devotion, and full moon rituals may feel especially potent. When perigee coincides with a new moon instead, some astrologers call it a super new moon, and new moon themes like intention-setting and fresh starts may feel more pronounced.

A micromoon, by contrast, falls at apogee. The full moon energy is still present but may feel softer or more subdued. Micromoons are not usually treated as a major factor in practice, but paying attention to how the distance lands for you can deepen your sense of connection to the lunar cycle.

If you notice a pull at the supermoon, try tracking perigee timing during other phases. You may find that orbital distance adds a subtle charge to whatever phase it overlaps with.

Blue Moons and Black Moons

Because the lunar cycle lasts about 29.5 days, slightly shorter than most calendar months, an extra full or new moon occasionally fits into one month or season. A repeated full moon is called a blue moon, and a repeated new moon is called a black moon.

There are three ways to define them:

  • Astronomical: When a season holds four full or new moons instead of the usual three, the third is the astronomical blue or black moon. This happens roughly every two to three years.
  • Calendrical: The second full or new moon within a single calendar month. This is the most commonly referenced definition in modern usage.
  • Astrological: The second full or new moon within a single zodiacal season. Not formally standardized, but it follows the same principle of repeated lunar energy within a defined window.

Some practitioners treat these moons as no different from any regular full or new moon, while others see them as amplified windows for revisiting intentions, getting a second chance on workings that did not land, or riding a wave of rare and concentrated energy. A blue moon is often associated with luck, success, and prophecy, while a black moon is linked to deep truth, shadow work, and long-range manifestation.

Each type of blue or black moon lends itself to a slightly different approach: calendrical ones suit self-made success and monthly goal-setting, astrological ones invite you to revisit the themes of a particular sign, and astronomical ones extend the window for working with seasonal and lunar energy together.

Monthly Moons

Each lunation through the year carries a traditional name tied to the season's character, from the animals and weather patterns to the harvests and shifts in light. Many of the names in common use today trace back to Algonquian peoples in North America, later adopted and adapted by colonial farmers. Others have Celtic, English, or broader Indigenous roots, and cultures around the world have developed their own names reflecting local seasonal rhythms.

A few things worth knowing as you explore them:

  • These names usually apply to the entire lunation, not just the full moon night. The whole cycle from new to full to dark carries the month's signature energy.
  • Because the lunar cycle runs about 29.5 days, slightly shorter than most calendar months, the same name can land in different months from year to year. The Harvest Moon, for instance, belongs to whichever full moon falls closest to the autumn equinox, so it may arrive in September or October. Some years also hold thirteen lunations instead of twelve.
  • Many of these names come from Indigenous traditions. If you work with them, take time to learn their origins and show genuine respect for the peoples and practices they come from. You might also research moon names local to the land where you live, and as your practice deepens, consider creating your own personal moon names that reflect your relationship with each season.

Connecting with the monthly moons is one of the simplest ways to align your magick with the turning year. Each lunation's themes, combined with the seasonal energy around it, offer a natural framework for timing spells, rituals, and reflective work.

Moon Sign Magick

As the Moon orbits Earth, she passes through sections of the sky associated with each zodiac sign, spending roughly two to three days in each one before moving on. In astrology, these transits are called moon signs, and in witchcraft they offer another layer of timing and intention for your spellwork.

The Moon holds a central place in Western astrology. She is associated with the classical element of water and represents the realms of feeling (both psychic and emotional), the subconscious, nurturing and being nurtured, daily habits, adaptability, and the most intimate parts of the self. Through the Moon, you can map your emotional and intuitive landscape, access the past, uncover repeating patterns, connect with ancestors, and bring hidden truths to the surface. In a birth chart, the Moon can reveal how you were raised and nurtured, and in turn how you nurture others.

Because the Moon shifts form slightly every day yet follows predictable patterns, she mirrors our own routines and our capacity to change. This makes moon magick especially effective for habit work: small, repeated shifts that build toward lasting transformation.

The Moon Through the Elements

As the Moon moves through each sign, she expresses her power through that sign's traits and themes. A quick elemental overview:

  • Fire signs (Aries, Leo, Sagittarius): The Moon's energy feels spontaneous and warm. This time favors vitality, courage, and self-expression.
  • Water signs (Cancer, Scorpio, Pisces): The Moon is in her home element and feels supportive and nurturing. Emotions flow freely, and connecting to feeling and intuition comes naturally.
  • Earth signs (Taurus, Virgo, Capricorn): The Moon's energy slows and steadies. Use this time to engage the physical senses, build structure, and promote long-lasting results.
  • Air signs (Gemini, Libra, Aquarius): The Moon illuminates the mind and inspires ideas. Communication, learning, and intellectual magick thrive here.

New Moons, Full Moons, and Signs

Because the new moon aligns with the Sun, it always falls in the same sign the Sun currently occupies. The full moon sits opposite the Sun, so it always lands in the opposite sign. If the Sun is in Libra, for example, the new moon will be a Libra new moon and the full moon will be in Aries. The Moon passes through all twelve signs during each lunation.

With a working knowledge of what the Moon means in each sign, you can specialize your full moon and new moon rituals, or combine sign energy with phase energy for precise timing. A first quarter moon in Taurus, for instance, carries a different charge than a first quarter moon in Sagittarius. The more you layer these rhythms together, the more nuanced and potent your practice becomes.

Your Moon Sign and Magick

Just as you have a sun sign, you also have a moon sign: the zodiac sign the Moon was in at the time of your birth. Your moon sign can reveal how you were nurtured or raised, how you prefer to be nurtured, and how you tend to nurture those closest to you. It can offer insight into your emotional and subconscious landscape, your sense of feeling, and perhaps even your soul, helping to guide and illuminate your purpose.

When it comes to magick, knowing your moon sign is not essential. But if you are able to access your birth chart (many free resources exist online), you may gain insight into what kind of magick is most comforting, healing, and nurturing for you personally. It can reveal the aspects of your intuitive and emotional nature that especially empower your lunar spells.

Astrology has many moving parts, and your moon sign is just one facet of a much larger puzzle. But reflecting on your own moon sign can be illuminating as you consider moon spells and how the Moon in each sign impacts you.

Eclipse Magick: To Do or Not to Do?

Eclipse magick is often treated with caution. Some practitioners avoid spellwork aimed at controlling outcomes during eclipses, describing the atmosphere as volatile or unpredictable. Others deliberately work with eclipse energy because it can feel amplified and catalytic.

A flexible approach is to prioritize practices that support clarity and realignment:

  • Meditation and grounding
  • Cleansing and energetic reset
  • Healing rites and restorative baths
  • Divination for insight, not certainty

If the energy feels chaotic, it can be wiser to focus on release and reflection rather than pushing the current. If the themes feel clear and you feel steady, you may choose to engage the power directly. In all cases, let your intuition guide the choice, and keep your work centered on alignment and healing.

Lunar Spellcasting

The moon moves through a constant rhythm of waxing and waning, and within that rhythm lies tremendous potential for your magick. Once you understand the meaning of each phase, the intensity of eclipses and supermoons, and the qualities the moon takes on as she moves through each zodiac sign, you may feel ready to dive straight into spellwork. Before you do, there are a few foundational principles worth knowing.

This section covers the essential building blocks for effective moon magick: from keeping a lunar grimoire and tending a lunar altar, to using affirmations and visualization to direct your intention and bring your spells to life.

Keeping a Lunar Grimoire

Many witches maintain a dedicated journal or notebook (sometimes called a grimoire or book of shadows) as a record of their magickal practice. This is the place to note spells that have worked well, information you want to be able to reference, and observations that help you track and deepen your spellcasting over time. Some witches prefer a casual, personal journal, while others opt for a binder that can be reorganized as their practice evolves. Whatever format suits you best is the right choice.

Tracking Your Personal Experiences with the Moon

A lunar grimoire becomes a resource you can return to again and again. The way the moon affects you is deeply individual. One sign might heighten stress for you, while another brings calm or a surge of confidence. Another witch might experience those same signs in the opposite way. Just as the moon reflects the sun's light, she also acts as a mirror for your inner world and outer circumstances.

Beginning to notice how particular phases and signs shape your mood, energy, and daily life can both strengthen your magick and deepen your personal relationship with the moon.

What to Record

To start noticing patterns, you'll need to know the moon's basic position at any given moment. Each time you sit down to journal, note:

  • What phase is the moon currently in?
  • What sign is the moon in, or is she void of course?
  • Are there any special lunar events occurring, such as an eclipse or a supermoon?

Many apps and websites track this information in real time. You can also find printed datebooks that list the moon's phase and sign for every day of the year. Once you're capturing this information consistently, you'll be able to look back and see what was happening in your life during particular placements, which spells you cast, and how they unfolded. Over time, the threads and themes of the moon's influence on your practice will begin to emerge naturally.

Recording Other Details

Beyond the moon's placement, there is plenty more you might choose to capture in your lunar grimoire, moon journal, or book of shadows. If tracking everything at once feels like too much, start with a single element, or focus on whatever feels most meaningful to you:

  • How are you feeling right now, emotionally and physically?
  • Are any significant life events unfolding at this time?
  • What spells are you casting, or what intentions are you actively working with?
  • What aspects of your lunar magick are going well? Is anything calling for adjustment?
  • Which herbal or crystal allies have felt most resonant? Which would you like to explore next?
  • What impressions arise during moon meditations, or simply when you pause to look up at the sky?
  • Are any recurring themes or patterns becoming visible in your life?

Write as much or as little as suits you. The moon is intimately connected to your emotional nature, and your grimoire should feel like an extension of that: organic, personal, and entirely your own. The more attention you give to the moon's influence, the more clearly those broader themes will emerge. Over time, your grimoire will also become a home for the lunar recipes, rituals, and spells that have proven their worth and deserve to be revisited.

Creating Your Lunar Altar

An altar is a sacred space for spellcasting, ritual, and meditation. Returning to the same space over time helps build up a charged, consecrated atmosphere that can deepen and amplify your lunar practice. That said, an altar is not a requirement. The earth itself is sacred ground, and witchcraft asks only that you work with what you have. When it comes to moon magick specifically, a dedicated space for casting lunar spells or charging crystals and ritual tools under moonlight can be a meaningful addition to your practice. It can be as modest as a repurposed tin or as expansive as a full table. Start with whatever is available to you.

Where to Set Up Your Altar

The ideal spot for a lunar altar is somewhere near a window. A windowsill where you can leave items to charge under moonlight is especially lovely, and if you can see the moon directly from that spot, it doubles as a natural meditation and reflection point. But no view is required. Any location will serve, and a moon symbol placed on your altar can always call that energy into the space regardless of visibility.

For those who need flexibility, a moveable altar is a practical and beautiful option. Many witches assemble travel altars inside small tins to carry on trips. A moveable setup might include a lunar symbol, incense, salt, and a crystal or two. A thrifted silver tray works particularly well: it provides a fire-safe surface for candles, and you can carry it outdoors to work under the moonlight, then bring it safely inside when you're done. Even a special cloth you unfold for spellwork counts as a moveable altar.

What to Place on Your Altar

These items make natural additions to a lunar altar and can support both meditation and spellcasting:

  • A lunar symbol: Artwork, a moon-shaped object, a tapestry, or even the tarot card The Moon can serve as a focal point that draws your attention to the moon's energy and invites reflection.
  • Incense: Scent is a powerful tool for shifting the mind into a meditative state and setting the atmosphere for ritual. Choose something calming, or select an incense with a specific lunar association.
  • A devotional candle: A candle lit only during moon magick, meditation, or lunar connection work (and snuffed out promptly when finished) builds a powerful energetic association over time. White and silver are traditional lunar colors, but follow your intuition. You might dress it with Moon Oil, cleanse it with Moon Water, or dust the top with lunar herbs.
  • A crystal: Stones like moonstone and selenite carry a natural resonance with lunar energy. Holding one while meditating can help attune your energy before working.
  • A tarot or oracle deck: The moon communicates readily through symbols. Pulling a daily card while working with lunar energy can offer meaningful insight into what the moon is reflecting back to you at any given moment.
  • A pendulum: A pendulum is a useful divination tool for receiving guidance, reading energy, and selecting lunar herbs or ingredients when you're uncertain which to use.

How to Use a Pendulum

Begin by establishing what "yes" and "no" look like for you. Hold the string or chain with your dominant hand, letting the charm hover over the palm of your nondominant hand. Ask the pendulum to show you "yes" and wait patiently for movement. Once you have a clear sense of that response, ask it to show you "no." You can repeat this calibration each time you work with it.

Common movement patterns include: clockwise for yes and counterclockwise for no, a vertical line for yes and horizontal for no, or a circle for yes and a diagonal line for no. Some people choose their own meanings in advance, or create a simple pendulum board by drawing "yes" and "no" on paper and letting the pendulum swing toward the written answer. Every practitioner's responses are a little different. Discovering your own is part of building a genuine connection with the tool.

As you settle into a lunar practice, you may feel drawn to set certain tools apart exclusively for moon magick. This is never required, but blessing and consecrating your tools to the moon can deepen their resonance and add another layer of intention to your ritual work. See the Lunar Tool Consecration Ritual in the Ritual Grimoire.

Get Ready to Perform Magick

Knowing the moon's phases, eclipses, seasonal cycles, and correspondences gives you a strong foundation, but before you begin spellwork, there are a few key techniques worth practicing. This section walks through how to prepare and plan for lunar spells, cleanse and ground your energy, and work with visualization. These principles apply to any moon spell or meditation, and as always, follow your intuition to find the approach that feels most natural to you.

Prepare Your Tools and Environment

Before reaching for your tools, take a moment to consider both your ingredients and your mindset. The environment you create shapes everything that follows. Think through these elements to build a calm, focused, and magickally supportive space:

  • Scent: What helps you feel centered? Incense, a mist, or an essential oil can shift your mental state quickly, easing you into a more receptive space for meditation or ritual.
  • Sound and music: Sound carries vibration, and vibration is the language of energy. A drum, rattle, or chant can anchor your focus, while a curated playlist or ambient music found online can provide a steady, immersive backdrop.
  • Comfort: It's hard to maintain focus when you're cold or uncomfortable. Lay out a blanket, cushion, or pillow before you begin so you won't need to break the flow of your ritual to tend to something basic.
  • Drink: A warm cup of tea or a glass of water is a simple but grounding ritual in itself. Breathing in the steam, feeling the warmth, and consciously hydrating before spellwork can help settle you into the work.
  • Light: Bright overhead light tends to be harsh and distracting. A small lamp, a cluster of candles, or even near-darkness can help soften the space and draw your attention inward toward the magick.
  • Visuals: Meditation doesn't require closed eyes. If you're visually oriented, consider an image of the moon, a meaningful painting, or even the tarot card The Moon as a focal point for your practice.
  • Touch and movement: If you're someone who connects through the body, hold a crystal whose texture and energy you love, or incorporate gentle movement before settling in. A slow neck roll, an abdominal rotation, or a quiet walk by moonlight can be a ritual in its own right.
  • Journaling: Keep your grimoire within reach. Writing down what's on your mind before you begin can help clear mental clutter, and having it nearby means you can capture any insights that arise during the working.

Once your altar and tools are assembled, you may wish to ritually prepare them before beginning, dedicating them to the moon's energy and the work ahead.

Prepare Your Mind and Energy

With your tools assembled and your environment ready, the next step is to prepare your inner landscape. Spellwork loses its potency when the mind is still tangled up in the events of the day. The following techniques help you quiet mental noise, clear energetic residue, and align yourself with the moon's rhythm before you begin.

Center Yourself

Centering calls your awareness back into your body and the present moment, quieting the mental chatter that spills over from daily life. Here's one simple approach:

  1. Take three slow, deep belly breaths. Feel your stomach expand as you inhale and contract as you exhale. Let the sound of your own breathing become your anchor.
  2. Hold each breath for a few seconds before releasing, resting in the stillness between inhale and exhale.
  3. As you breathe out, let your shoulders soften. Notice the brief silence after each exhale before the next breath begins. With each cycle, your awareness settles more fully into your body.
  4. Bring your focus to the solar plexus, the energy center just below the breastbone, slightly above the navel. Breathe in for four counts, hold for four, exhale for four. Adjust the counts to whatever rhythm feels most natural. With each breath, sense that center glowing with warmth and energy.

Cleanse Your Energy

Throughout the day, you naturally absorb energies from the people and places around you, sometimes forming unconscious energetic cords in the process. Before meditation or spellwork, it's worth clearing this accumulated residue. Think of it as an energetic bath. Some effective methods:

  • Selenite wand: Selenite is named after the moon goddess Selene, making it a particularly fitting tool for lunar work. Slowly trace the wand around your body, giving extra attention to the back of your neck, crown of your head, and heart center. Move with intention and notice any subtle shifts as you work.
  • Cleansing spray: Mists containing cleansing essences like lemon can clear both your aura and your space quickly. You can also craft your own by combining purified or spring water, essential oils, and a splash of alcohol.
  • Herb smoke: Burn the tip of a dried herb sprig or a purpose-made bundle and let the smoke drift through your space. Rosemary is a reliable choice. Open a window for ventilation and be mindful of smoke alarms.
  • Breath: Use your breath as an energetic broom. Inhale cleansing, clear energy and exhale anything you're ready to release, including unwanted thoughts, emotions, or psychic debris.
  • Water: Water is deeply connected to the moon and carries natural cleansing properties. Spritz salt water around yourself, touch it to your skin, or visualize a stream of cool, clear water washing away whatever you no longer need.

Ground Yourself

Grounding anchors your awareness in the physical world and keeps you from being swept away by the intensity of lunar energy, which can stir up deep, vulnerable emotions. It also ensures that the energy you work with during ritual lands in a tangible, real way rather than dissipating into abstraction. Some approaches:

  • Go barefoot outside: The simplest and most direct grounding technique. Stand or walk on grass, soil, sand, or stone. Feel the texture and temperature beneath your feet and let your awareness drop down into the earth.
  • Hold a grounding stone: Hematite or black tourmaline are classic choices. Hold the stone, breathe deeply, and bring your attention to wherever your body meets a solid surface. You may begin to feel the subtle pulse of the earth beneath you.
  • Visualize a grounding cord: Imagine a root or beam of energy extending from the base of your spine deep into the earth's core. With each breath, draw nourishing earth energy up through this cord and let any excess or unwanted energy flow back down. This technique not only connects you to the earth but can actively replenish your energy so your spellwork draws from that source rather than depleting you.

Connect to the Moon

Once you are centered, cleansed, and grounded, you are ready to open to the moon. Go outside or find a window and simply look up. Take in the stars and the moon, and let yourself feel small in the best possible way, part of something vast and ancient. Hold a lunar crystal like moonstone or selenite if you have one nearby.

If the moon isn't visible, you can still make this connection inwardly. Picture yourself as a tree: your roots reaching deep into the earth through your grounding cord, and your branches stretching upward toward the moon. Or visualize a column of silver light descending from the moon and flowing through the crown of your head, filling your body with her energy. Feel the moon's gravitational pull on you, because it is real, and you are part of this same system of tides.

Working with Energy

Once you have a grounding and centering practice in place, learning to sense and send energy becomes the next meaningful step. Being able to feel energy allows you to communicate your intentions to plant spirits, crystal allies, and the forces you call upon in your lunar workings.

Sensing Crystal Energy

Hold a stone in your hand and slow your breathing. Gently bring your awareness to where the stone rests against your palm. You may notice a subtle hum or vibration, or a quiet shift somewhere in your body. Try this with several stones, one at a time, taking deep breaths and tuning in slowly. Some crystals may feel like nothing at first; others may connect with you immediately. Both responses are valid and informative.

Feeling Auras and Energetic Boundaries

Everything has an energy that surrounds it, often called an aura. As you draw closer to that field, the energy tends to grow denser and more defined. One way to begin recognizing what an aura feels like is to work with plants and crystals as practice partners. Go outside or gather a few crystals of different sizes. Hold your hand several feet away from a crystal or plant, then bring it in slowly, paying close attention to any point where you feel a shift. A soft buzzing or increased density of energy is common as your palm draws near.

Sending Energy

Sending energy is how you communicate your intentions to plant spirits, crystal allies, or other forces in your magickal work. Before attempting this, complete one of the centering and grounding practices described above. This ensures you are drawing from an external source rather than depleting your own reserves.

Visualize branches growing from your head and shoulders, reaching all the way up toward the moon and beyond into the cosmos. Just as leaves photosynthesize sunlight, the leaves of your branches gather ethereal moonlight and starlight, drawing that energy back down through you. If this image feels complex, simply visualize a beam of silver lunar light descending from the sky and flowing down through your head and arms.

Once you feel that energy moving through you, channel it outward with a clear intention. You might assign the energy a color that corresponds to your desired outcome, or simply hold your goal clearly in mind as you direct it toward a crystal or plant ally. You may notice a subtle response from them as you do so, or you can visualize your ally attuning to the energy the way a night-blooming flower opens toward the moon.

These techniques sharpen your ability to discern different qualities of energy, recognize when your tools are aligned with your intentions, and assess where your spells may need additional support.

Affirmations and Visualization

Even with solid preparation, we sometimes get in our own way. A spell cast with doubt, or without mental and physical space for the outcome to take root, often falls flat. Two practices that directly address this are affirmations and visualization. Used consistently, they become spells in their own right.

Write a Moon Affirmation

An affirmation is a statement repeated aloud or internally, phrased to affirm your desired mood, feeling, or result. Writing and repeating one throughout the lunar cycle helps align your mind and energy with your intentions and creates room for them to manifest.

Begin with what you want to bring into your life. Jot down a word or phrase, or simply write the desire plainly. Then get more specific. Is there a purpose behind it? A particular form you want it to take? Think about the quality of energy you want it to carry, something that flows freely, or arrives with ease.

Next, write the intention as though it is already happening, from a positive and confident perspective. "Money flows effortlessly and freely to me. I have plenty to cover my needs, save extra, and afford what I want" is more anchored than a vague wish. When an affirmation resonates, you will feel it land in your body.

Decide how often to repeat it. Twice daily is a reliable baseline, but at the start of a new cycle, more frequent repetition helps create the mental and energetic space your spell needs to take hold. Write the final version on its own piece of paper. If you like, anoint it with Moon Oil and place it somewhere you will see it daily, such as a bathroom mirror, so you can say it while preparing for the day and winding down at night.

Repeat the affirmation throughout the waxing phase, adjusting the wording as needed. If desired, burn the paper at the full moon as a release.

To deepen the practice, pair your affirmation with a magickal anchor: hold a crystal aligned with your intention, spray a mist or perfume as you speak the words, or connect the affirmation to a specific symbol, sigil, or charm. Keeping that object visible reinforces the working between formal practice sessions.

Visualization

Visualization is exactly what it sounds like: imagining how something might look or feel if it were already real. In magickal practice, conscious visualization is a powerful way to attune yourself to the energy of your desired outcome and call it toward you. It works especially well for visual and kinesthetic learners, and the key is to stay open to alternate possibilities as circumstances evolve.

When you visualize a goal, manifestation, or spell outcome as though it has already come true, you align your own energy with that result, supporting the intentions you cast at the new moon. Here is one approach:

  1. Begin by cleansing your energy, or clear mental clutter by writing your thoughts out on paper. When ready, close your eyes and breathe deeply.
  2. Bring your desired outcome to mind. Visualize it unfolding. How does it feel in your body? Connect fully with that emotion.
  3. Focus on the end result rather than the mechanics of how it arrives. Feel it with your whole body. Engage your senses: what will you see, hear, smell, taste, or feel when this is real?
  4. Continue until joy or excitement rises naturally in your body. When you feel ready, breathe that energy and that vision into every part of yourself.

Visualization is especially useful during the waxing phase or immediately before a spell, though it supports any moon effort. Returning to it daily allows the details of your manifestation to become clearer and more tangible over time.

Traditionally, birthstones are crystals associated with zodiac signs based on ancient correspondences. Sacred Creature

The crab is the creature assigned to Cancer, the only astrological sign belonging exclusively to the moon. Those born under Cancer are believed to resemble crabs in temperament. In Mediterranean regions, crabs and crayfish are intensely affiliated with the moon and considered lunar foods that transmit the moon's effects and impart psychic power.

The Crab

The constellation we call Cancer has not always worn the shape of a crab, yet whatever creature has stood for it, the shell has remained a constant. Early European astrologers drew it as a crayfish, while the Egyptians saw the scarab beetle, a sacred emblem of death and rebirth and the sign of the god Khepera. Even so, the words for the constellation in Persian, Greek, Sanskrit, and Babylonian all carry the meaning of crab. This may have been the most significant figure in the whole zodiac, for it holds more fixed stars within its reach than any other sign. The Maya were not alone in expecting the world to end when the planets gathered here; the Romans, too, held that Juno had set Cancer in the heavens to mark the end of all things whenever she chose to bring it about.

The Glyph

The well-known "69" shorthand for Cancer invites several readings. It is built from two matching parts set in opposite positions, and to some this see-saw shape mirrors the up-and-down moods often linked to the sign. Since the constellation rises just after the summer solstice, as the seasons turn, the paired spirals can be taken to mark that change. Others see two spermatozoa meeting to form a single seed, tying the sign once more to conception and birth, or read the figure as a pair of breasts in keeping with its themes of nurture and fertility. Still others see fixed stars of the constellation itself, one turned upward and one down, an image of the principle "as above, so below."

Qualities

Cancer arrives just as the seasons shift and the Sun's climb tips over into decline. A lunar sign of the water element, it is held to be passive, home-loving, imaginative, romantic, and at times self-absorbed. The Moon's influence lends a vivid imagination and a depth of inner life, both fitting the sign well. Every creature ever tied to this constellation shares a single feature, the shell, an emblem of self-protection that speaks to the guarded, withdrawn streak in some born under Cancer. The sign rules the very parts that such a shell would shield: the heart, the lungs, and the stomach.

This same power appears across world traditions under different names: Hermes to the Greeks, Thoth to the Egyptians, Odin to the Scandinavians, and Woden to the early Anglo-Saxons, who called it Earendel, the Morning Star. The Moon in Myth and Symbol

Because the Moon is lit at night by the Sun's light, it carries all the positive and negative traits associated with the female. Seen more widely, without the Sun's light none of the planets in our solar system would be illuminated and life on Earth would not exist as we know it, so the Earth shares a kind of sisterhood with the Moon, both relying on the Sun to be seen.

The Moon is visible chiefly at night, and night is bound up with death, so it made sense to our ancestors that the souls of the dead must dwell in the lunar atmosphere, an old belief that caused some unease at the time of the first Moon landings. Where the Sun's light stands for intuition and deductive reasoning, the Moon, as a mirror of the Sun, signifies knowledge gathered in a more inductive and painstaking way. The owl, a nocturnal bird that shares the Moon's symbolic space, is therefore the bird of knowledge. By its color the Moon is linked to the metal silver.

In human beings the female menstrual cycle echoes the cycle of the Moon. Traditionally women menstruated at the new Moon and ovulated at the full, though artificial light and manmade surroundings mean the two no longer always align. The word menstruation comes from the Greek mene, meaning Moon, a word that also gives us month, even though we measure months by a solar reckoning as well as a lunar one.

The Fish

Both the Greeks and the Persians called this constellation the Fish, while the Babylonians knew it as Two Tails and split the star cluster into two separate shapes, Simmah the swallow and Anunitum the goddess. The symbol for Pisces is traditionally a pair of fish swimming in opposite directions, their mouths nonetheless joined by a cord. That cord is faint within the actual constellation yet still visible; the Babylonians called it Riksu and the Arabians Al Risha, and it is a vital part of the sign that has long carried esoteric significance.

The Glyph

The sigil for the fish comes from Egyptian sources and has scarcely changed since, unlike the glyphs of other constellations. The original Egyptian sign showed the two opposing curves, but kept them separate; the connecting line was added in the fourteenth or fifteenth century, giving the symbol its present H shape.

The Water of the Fish

Though some modern readings of Pisces leave out the cord, the fact that the fish are joined rather than parted matters a great deal, a fine demonstration of how a seemingly simple line within a symbol can hold so much meaning. The duality of the fish is well known, even if it signifies different things, such as the soul that craves the stimulus of the material world and the spirit that longs to leave such things behind, neither of which can survive without the other. This spirit and soul significance carries into seventeenth-century alchemical writings. Because of their tie to water, fish are symbols of the Goddess and the feminine aspect, and some say the fish swimming in opposite directions point to the supposed female difficulty in reaching a decision, or to the experience, shared by both sexes, of being pulled in two directions at once. Since the fish is so closely aligned with the Christian faith, the Pisces symbol is sometimes found in churches where no other astrological imagery appears, and Christ was born at the start of the Age of Pisces. Those born under the sign are said to be dreamy and impractical, deep thinkers drawn to psychic matters.
