The Virgin

For all that her name suggests, Virgo has worn many guises across the long ages since the zodiac was first mapped, from the chaste maiden to the wanton temptress and every shade of the feminine that lies between. She has been named for many goddesses. To the Romans she was Ceres, cradling a sheaf of corn as a token of fertility and the harvest, and indeed Virgo rises just as the crops are gathered in. The Egyptians tied her to Isis and to Maat, goddess of truth. Every name given to her speaks of the Virgin or the Maiden.

A Greek tale connects her with Astraea, goddess of truth and virtue, who once dwelt among mortals alongside the other immortals. When Pandora loosed every kind of misery upon the world, life on Earth grew unbearable, and though Astraea lingered as long as she could endure it, she was the last of the deities to depart, her finer nature wounded by human conduct. Tarot Origins

For centuries, seekers have turned to this beautiful oracle for guidance, insight, and answers to life's pressing questions. While the tarot's true origins remain shrouded in mystery, several theories attempt to trace its roots.

Theories of Origin

Some scholars believe the cards date back over two millennia to ancient Egypt and the legendary library of Alexandria. Others suggest the Crusaders carried them westward from the Middle East. A third tradition credits the Romani people with introducing tarot to Europe.

Further Theories and Suppression

To the Scottish ministers who denounced it, the deck was nothing less than the Devil's Picture Book, and for long stretches of its past the Christian establishment eyed it with unease. The cards kept their pull regardless, bound up with the old streams of hidden knowledge, the Kabbalah, the craft of witches, the pagan ways, and alchemy among them, and they held their place as an instrument of divination wired to the planets and the signs. To Carl Jung, their pictures were a parade of the deep, shared figures of the psyche.

That a thing called arcana, a word for the secret and the concealed, should have murky beginnings is only fitting. Lineages have been claimed for it running back to Hermes Trismegistus, reputed father of alchemy, and to Egypt, India, Arabia, and China by turns. By one telling the Knights Templar brought the deck west, its pictures a screen for Saracen magickal teaching kept clear of a Church quick to persecute, and the knight was struck from the ordinary pack so the Templar link would go unnoticed. Medieval churchmen suspected the cards of spreading the Gnostic doctrines of the Cathar heretics, and across the years from 1378 to 1450 they fell under bans in Regensburg, Marseilles, Paris, Siena, Venice, and the north of Italy. Later the same Church set about bending them toward Christian teaching, just as it had once swallowed the lore of the Zodiac.

The scholar Court de Gebelin, much occupied with the deck, held the name to be Egyptian in root, joining Tar for road with Ro for royal, so that the word announced a royal road toward wisdom. A second guess hangs on the palindrome ROTA TARO ORAT TORA ATOR, taken to mean that the wheel of the taro tells of the law of Hathor.

Renaissance Card Games of the Rich and Famous

Whether these origin theories hold truth cannot be said with certainty. What is known is that tarot shares a clear lineage with Renaissance playing cards, with similarities still visible in modern poker decks.

Italy's Tarocchi

During the 1400s, Italian nobility played a game called Il Trionfos using cards known as trionfi (triumphs). Wealthy patrons commissioned artists to create these cards, either hand-painted or printed using carved woodblocks.

These weren't simple gambling games. They were creative exercises where players drew inspiration from the card imagery to compose poems about one another. The oldest surviving deck is also among the most exquisite: the Visconti Tarot, commissioned by the Duke of Milan in the mid-fifteenth century. Many original cards from this deck, painted on gold and silver foil, now reside in New York's Morgan Library & Museum.

Islamic Card Games

Card games flourished in the Arab world during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, particularly among the wealthy and military elite. The Mamluk pack significantly influenced modern tarot. This deck contained:

  • Four suits: coins, cups, swords, and polo sticks
  • Ten numbered cards per suit
  • Four court cards per suit

Sound familiar? This structure mirrors today's Minor Arcana. The cards likely served both gaming and fortune-telling purposes, as evidenced by prognosticating rhymes inscribed on them:

As for the present that rejoices, thy heart will soon open up.
O thou who hast possessions, remain happy and thou shalt have a pleasant life.
With the sword of happiness I shall redeem a beloved who will afterwards take my life.

The remaining original cards are housed in Istanbul's Topkapi Museum. Images are viewable at World of Playing Cards.

The Spanish Card Game of Love

Fifteenth-century Spanish nobility played Juego de Naypes with forty-nine colorful cards designed for fortune-telling and revealing secrets, especially romantic ones. The deck featured four suits based on women: maidens, wives, widows, and nuns. Each card revealed what someone loved or desired most, with verses matching the card's number in line count.

By the seventeenth century, professional cartomancers (card-reading fortune-tellers) practiced their craft throughout Spain, laying out cards in patterns resembling modern tarot spreads.

Tarot in the Modern Era

Early tarot decks, though beautifully designed, often lacked the narrative imagery familiar to modern readers, making interpretation more challenging. The turn of the twentieth century brought renewed enthusiasm for the tarot alongside growing interest in Spiritualism and ritual magick, along with an entirely new approach to the cards.

The Tarot's Two Books

Modern tarot decks comprise two "books": the Major Arcana and Minor Arcana. The word arcana means "mysteries" or "secrets."

ArcanaCardsStructure
Minor56 cardsFour suits with 10 numbered cards + 4 court cards each
Major22 cardsNumbered 0 (The Fool) through 21 (The World)

The Minor Arcana resembles both Renaissance playing cards and modern poker decks (though poker has only three court cards per suit). Minor Arcana cards describe everyday events and experiences, while Major Arcana cards reveal cosmic, spiritual, or divine forces (destiny itself) at work.

The Rider-Waite-Smith Deck

In 1909, tarot underwent a transformative shift. Arthur Edward Waite, a prominent occultist, commissioned Pamela Colman Smith, an artist and theatrical designer, to create a unique deck. Both belonged to the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, an influential mystical society Waite would eventually lead as Grand Master. This affiliation explains the deck's Golden Dawn symbolism.

Under Waite's direction, Smith painted seventy-eight images that became the tarot cards published by William Rider & Son in 1910.

The deck's revolutionary feature? All cards, not just the Major Arcana, depicted storytelling scenes conveying their meanings. Readers could now interpret cards intuitively through imagery alone. The Ten of Swords shows a figure lying face-down with ten swords in their back, instantly evoking treachery, deception, and pain. The Three of Cups depicts joyful women dancing together, clearly celebrating friendship and happy times.

Over a century later, the Rider-Waite-Smith tarot remains the most popular and influential deck worldwide.

The Thoth Tarot

Opinions on the Thoth Tarot tend to be polarized. Painted by Lady Frieda Harris under direction from the notorious English occultist Aleister Crowley between 1938 and 1943, its striking imagery and vivid colors captivate some tarotists while unsettling others. This is fitting, given its controversial creator.

Though not published until 1969 (after both Crowley and Harris had died), it has remained continuously in print ever since.

The Thoth Tarot draws on diverse esoteric, scientific, spiritual, and philosophical traditions including alchemy, astrology, and ceremonial magick. (Thoth was an Egyptian deity who served as scribe to the gods.) Crowley renamed some Major Arcana cards, calling card fourteen "Art" instead of "Temperance," for instance. He also altered court card titles, which some readers find confusing.

Tarot Innovations

Today, tens of thousands of tarot decks exist, with artists continuously creating more. Whatever your heritage, interests, or aesthetic preferences (Celtic, Japanese, Native American, gardening, baseball, cats, unicorns, vampires, zombies, or even gummy bears), a deck exists that speaks to you.

While most tarot cards are rectangular, the Motherpeace Tarot features round cards. Emerging in the 1970s alongside feminism's rise, it celebrates 30,000 years of women's culture. Some decks feature oversized Renaissance-style cards; others are pocket-sized miniatures. Some include extra cards beyond the standard seventy-eight, or blank cards for personal creation. Many come with companion books explaining interpretations according to the designer's philosophy.

Original unpublished decks can be viewed online. Blogs and social media groups offer vibrant forums for enthusiasts to share ideas. Free instant readings are available online. As technology evolves, the tarot (a living, evolving medium) will undoubtedly continue to innovate.

Magick, Witchcraft, and the Tarot

Perhaps you've practiced witchcraft for years and recently discovered tarot. Or maybe tarot readings guided you into the witches' world. However you arrived here, whatever inspired this path: welcome!

Not all witches work with tarot, but many do. As explored in the introduction, tarot and witchcraft share deep connections. The Magician card displays four tools witches use in magickal practice: wand, chalice, pentagram, and sword/athame. The magus raises one hand skyward and points the other earthward, embodying the axiom "as above, so below" and the union of heaven and earth. Some decks also feature these four tools on The World card.

The four Minor Arcana suits take their names from these tools, symbolizing the four elements witches recognize as fundamental energetic forces:

Witches also associate the four elements with the cardinal directions and the four archangels:

When casting a circle for ritual or magickal work, you may invoke these archangels and evoke elemental powers. Examine The World card in the Rider-Waite-Smith deck: winged elemental symbols appear in the corners, representing the archangels and universal forces. The same might be said of the tarot.

The Arcana and Their Hidden Order

The four lesser suits sort themselves not only by element but by charge. Fire in the Wands and air in the Swords run to the active and the masculine, while water in the Cups and earth in the Coins or Pentacles run to the receptive and the feminine. One reading threads the suits through four life-stages borrowed from Tantric thought: Sambhoga, the season of pleasure, where the cup first takes on the taste of experience; Nirmana, the constructive years of early adulthood, signed by the wand, scepter, or vajra; Artha, the heaping-up of worldly goods in the suit of coins; and Moksha, release and the practice of dying well, borne by the sword as the emblem of letting go.

The twenty-two trumps of the Major Arcana have earned the title quintessence of occultism, their images paired with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. That same twenty-two counts the paths strung between the Sephiroth on the Tree of Life, and a number of the cards mirror the Sephiroth in turn, reaching from the Fool as the shapeless void of the Ain Soph to the Wheel of Fortune as the Kingdom. They keep company with the Zodiac too: the Lovers with Gemini, the Moon with the crab or lobster of Cancer, Strength with the lion of Leo. Readers often bundle the twenty-one numbered trumps into three sevens, the first for spirit, the next for soul, the last for the world of matter, leaving the Fool to stand alone with no number at all.

Tarot Basics & Myths

A tarot deck functions as a tool, and like any tool it carries real limitations. It serves readings, meditation, self-exploration, guidance, and even play, but it cannot perform tasks outside that scope, the same way a hammer outperforms a deck of cards when driving a nail.

What Tarot Can and Cannot Do

Approaches to the deck vary widely, and no single method stands as the only correct one. Some readers treat tarot as sacred, building ritual and dedicated space around its use, or centering an entire magickal practice on the cards without ever using them for divination. Others approach the deck intellectually, exploring the psyche through its pictures and symbols. Some use it within healing or counseling work, while others read only for themselves in a purely intuitive manner. The practice takes the shape of whoever works with it.

Cards can aid in solving problems, offer new perspective on a situation, support meditation, or map a path forward. They can also mark the start of a professional practice built around helping others at pivotal moments.

A genuine, holistic reading stays as positive and healing as possible, even when a querent faces a difficult period. The harder cards in a deck deserve full attention rather than avoidance, holding space for both reader and querent through rocky passages.

Skill with the cards grows in direct proportion to time invested, the same as any other practiced craft. A deck will not clean a house or cook a meal, but its capacity to transform inner and outer experience remains remarkable for a simple set of cards.

Understanding Tarot Reversals

A tarot reversal occurs when a card appears upside down in a reading. Cards become reversed through shuffling, whether that happens naturally or a reader intentionally shuffles some cards into the deck reversed. Some readers work fluently with reversals, while others simply turn a reversed card upright and read only its upright meaning.

Reversed meanings often represent underlying issues, blocked energy, or delays in a card's influence on the reading. They can also point to a key energy that has yet to manifest or that has been diminished. This nuanced approach deepens personal introspection, acknowledging the many sided nature of a situation and encouraging consideration of different perspectives and underlying factors within the querent's story.

Whether a reader learns and works with reversed meanings comes down to individual style and preference. Some readers learn upright and reversed meanings side by side. Others build a solid foundation in upright meanings first and return to reversals later. Still other readers work only with upright cards, trusting that a reading's message comes through regardless of a card's orientation.

Both upright and reversed meanings appear throughout the card descriptions in this grimoire, enriching understanding of how each card can manifest in a reading. New readers are encouraged to practice with upright meanings alone for a while before incorporating reversals, gradually finding what approach works best with experience.

Tarot Myths Debunked

Common misconceptions about tarot persist widely, rooted largely in old stereotypes and religious rhetoric that outlived their original context. Some myths circulate even among readers themselves. Fact-check any claim that feels off.

Myth: A Tarot Deck Must Be Gifted, Never Bought

This enduring belief has no real basis. The best judge of which deck to work with is the reader. A gifted deck whose imagery fails to resonate can be genuinely frustrating to use. Any deck taken up for practice should feel personally inspiring, so buying a first, second, or third deck directly is entirely appropriate.

Myth: Tarot Is Evil, Linked to Dark Magick and Possession

This idea traces back to religious belief and outdated popular portrayals of tarot readers. The deck reflects the full range of life, including its challenging and taboo aspects, the same way life itself holds both ease and struggle. No tool carries inherent evil. Tarot is neutral and reflects the intentions of whoever uses it. A small number of people, generally those unfamiliar with actual tarot practice, believe the cards themselves hold power or attached spirits. In truth, the cards are simply cards, and meaning comes from interpretation. Ceremonial decks and alchemical symbolism appearing on some cards do not make them nefarious. They simply reflect esoteric design traditions that unfamiliarity tends to make suspect.

Myth: Tarot Cannot Be Read for Friends and Family

No rule restricts who may receive a reading. Friends and family who welcome a reading make excellent practice querents. Increased familiarity with someone's life can introduce bias over time, and delivering difficult truths to someone close can be uniquely hard, at which point referring them to another reader becomes reasonable. Anyone learning tarot should expect requests for readings once others find out, and should feel free to decline any reading that feels premature or uncomfortable.

Myth: Reading Tarot Requires Psychic Ability

Some psychics use tarot, but reading skill is learnable by anyone. Interpretation style remains a personal matter, and while intuitive ability often grows through consistent work with the cards, no baseline psychic gift is required to read effectively.

Myth: Drawing the Death Card Predicts Literal Death

If this were true, tarot events would be far more dangerous than they are. The Death card typically signals transformation, change, or the close of a phase rather than physical death. Genuine correlations with physical death are rare and generally coincide with an already known illness or an approaching end of life. The card marks a natural part of life's cycle rather than an omen of doom.

Myth: Self-Readings Are Always Inaccurate

Opinion divides on this point. Some readers avoid self-readings, believing personal investment distorts interpretation, while many others find real value in reading for themselves. Awareness of one's own closeness to a situation determines whether outside perspective would help. Daily draws and reflective self-readings remain valuable tools for learning card meanings and gaining insight into personal circumstances.

Myth: Predictions Are Set in Stone

Predictive readings describe potential outcomes based on current circumstances, not a fixed future. Decisions and actions taken afterward can shift the outcome described.

Myth: Skilled Readers Achieve Full Accuracy

No reader, regardless of experience, achieves complete accuracy, particularly in predictive work. Claims of perfect accuracy reflect overconfidence rather than reality.

Myth: Tarot Belongs to Specific Religions or Occult Traditions

Tarot originated as a card game and evolved into a flexible tool unbound by any single religious or occult framework. It adapts to whatever spiritual or secular context its user brings to it.

Myth: Only Professionals Read Accurately

Reading skill is not restricted to professionals. Accuracy depends far more on a reader's interpretive ability and a querent's openness than on professional status.

Myth: Certain Cards Always Predict Bad Outcomes

Cards such as Death, the Tower, and the Devil carry reputations for doom, but their meanings span a wide range, including liberation, transformation, and the shedding of old patterns.

Tarot functions as a card system suited to many kinds of readings and as a meaningful aid within magickal and ritual work. It does not fix a future in place. Free will and personal choice continue to shape outcomes moment to moment. Skepticism from others rarely shifts through argument alone, and continued growth as a reader over time remains the strongest response.

Tips for Reading and Interpreting the Cards

Reading tarot is a multifaceted skill, and there's no single right way to engage with a card or a spread. As you build experience, starting with single-card draws and working outward, the approaches below can help you unpack a card's meaning from different angles. Some will resonate with you more than others, and that's expected; everyone lands on their own mix of techniques that clicks.

Technique One: First Impressions

Start simply by looking at the card and noticing what draws your eye first — a figure, an object, a color. That initial impression often carries useful information. Ask yourself what caught your attention first and what it might suggest about the card's meaning.

Technique Two: Color Theory

Color choices in tarot carry symbolic weight rather than being purely decorative. Notice the dominant colors on a card — does red suggest passion or aggression? Does blue suggest calm or emotional depth? Consider what the card's color palette adds to its meaning.

Technique Three: Numbers Matter

Each number carries its own symbolic and vibrational quality — ones often point to beginnings, tens to completions, and so on. Ask what the card's number might reveal about cyclical patterns or key stages in your (or your querent's) life.

Technique Four: Figures and Symbols

Notice the human figures or animals shown on the card and what they're doing. Each carries its own symbolism and story that can point toward the energies or actions tied to the card's meaning.

Technique Five: Environment and Background

A card's setting — a garden, a desert, a battlefield — sets an emotional tone that's as informative as its figures. Ask whether the environment feels welcoming or unsettling, and let that inform the overall energy the card brings to a reading.

Technique Six: Symbols

Every symbol included on a card is intentional and often carries layered meaning. Reflect on the symbols you notice and where else you've seen them before, and consider their origins for a deeper reading.

Working through these questions invites ongoing rediscovery of your deck; even familiar cards can reveal something new. This approach deepens both your readings and your personal relationship with the cards, and it's especially useful when getting to know a new deck or one with unfamiliar imagery.

Preparing for a Tarot Reading

Every reader develops their own approach to preparing for and conducting readings, whether for themselves or others. Some build rituals around their practice and treat the cards as part of a larger spiritual discipline; others do nothing special before a reading. Preferences around space vary too: some readers want a dedicated reading space, while others read wherever and whenever.

Much of this comes down to personal style, but practicality plays a role as well. Reading in a crowded, loud venue might be genuinely difficult for a highly sensitive or empathic reader, yet if you've committed to reading at an event, you work with the setting you're given.

Exercise Six: What Kind of Tarot Reader Will I Be?

These questions can help you explore your own preferences as a reader. There are no right or wrong answers, and your answers may shift as you grow into the practice. Something that sounds ideal in theory doesn't always feel right once you try it. Experiment with different settings and rituals before and after your readings to find your own fit.

  • Do I have a spiritual practice, and would tarot be part of it?
  • What atmosphere do I want to create for my readings?
  • What parts of my personality do I want to bring into my readings?
  • Do I want to read for others, or just for myself?
  • Will I stick with one deck, or use several?
  • Where would I love to do my readings?
  • Are there places I know I don't want to read cards?
  • Do I have any other preferences for my reading environment?
  • Am I comfortable with others touching my deck, or do I want to be the only one who does?

Exercise Seven: Grounding and Centering Techniques

Grounding and centering practices stabilize your energy, reconnect you with your body, and bring you back into the present moment. Doing this after a reading helps close down any energy you opened during the session and signals to your mind and body that it's complete, which is especially useful if a reading leaves you feeling drained.

Below is a simple practice you can use before or after a reading. It may take a few tries before it really lands, so don't worry if you don't feel much the first time. Some readers like to hold a grounding stone, such as black tourmaline or hematite, during this exercise.

  1. Sit comfortably with your feet flat on the ground, barefoot if you can. Rest your hands in your lap and close your eyes gently.
  2. Bring your attention to your breath, in through the nose and out through the mouth, without forcing it. Let your focus settle at the soles of your feet; a little warmth or tingling there is normal.
  3. Picture roots growing from the bottom of your feet (or wherever your body touches the ground) deep into the earth: your foundation and connection to groundedness and security.
  4. With every breath, imagine those roots reaching deeper, drawing up energy and nourishment. Sit with that connection for a few breaths, even if you can't picture it vividly.
  5. Shift your attention to the crown of your head, imagining branches reaching upward into the sky, full of leaves catching sunlight and moving in the breeze, clearing any mental fog as they sway.
  6. Feel yourself connected to earth below and sky above, centered between them. With each inhale, draw in whatever healing or energy you need; with each exhale, release anything you're ready to let go of back into the earth to be transformed. Let the element of air clear your mind of intrusive thoughts.
  7. Offer a quiet thanks to the elements and whatever guides or higher forces resonate with you. Let your branches settle back into your body and your roots return to your feet. When you're ready, open your eyes. Consider jotting down what you experienced, and make sure to eat and drink something afterward.

Significator Cards

Significator cards are intentionally selected from the tarot deck to represent the querent in a reading. Usually, the card chosen represents the querent's zodiac sign or matches their personality. Selecting a significator card can anchor the reading around that person, letting you see how the significator interacts with the other cards drawn. Using a significator is especially helpful when reading without your querent physically present, keeping your focus on them throughout a remote reading.

Significator cards can help place your querent inside the reading by visually representing them, showing how the symbols in the reading or the other people involved affect them. Using a significator lets you see whether the surrounding energies are oppressive or supportive and how they interact with each other, giving you a clear visual snapshot of what's happening immediately around the reading's subject.

Selecting a significator card is straightforward. Find out your querent's zodiac sign, then choose the court card connected to that sign, usually the one matching their sun sign. What matters is the dignity the card represents, not the physical appearance of the figure on it.

Another approach is to pull the page, knight, queen, and king from the suit tied to your querent's zodiac sign. For example, for Taurus, an earth sign, pull the Page, Knight, Queen, and King of Pentacles, then show your querent all four and ask which one feels most like them. They don't need any tarot knowledge to answer.

Depending on a deck's artwork, you may not always like the card you'd typically use as your own significator. If that happens, feel free to pick a different card that better fits how you see yourself.

Once you've chosen a significator card, place it in the reading. Many readers set it in the center of the table and build the spread around it, so they can see what's opposing, above, below, and surrounding the querent. Others place it at the top of the table, separate from the spread itself.

Notice whether readings feel different with a significator card versus without one, and experiment to see what works for you. Significator cards should add value to your readings, not stress. If they feel distracting or unnecessary, there's no obligation to use them.

Why Playing Cards?

Playing cards are among the most accessible and historically grounded tools available for divination and spellwork. Long before mass-produced tarot decks lined bookstore shelves, everyday people reached for what they had on hand. European peasants practiced magick with kitchen knives, local herbs, and still water, not ritual swords or exotic imports. A deck of cards fit that same tradition perfectly. Even before modern manufacturing, playing cards were easier to obtain than any tarot deck, and today they can be found at gas stations, grocery stores, and dollar shops.

A Legitimate Magickal Tradition

Playing cards carry a history as deep as the tarot. Their four suits, Hearts, Clubs, Diamonds, and Spades, encode elemental symbolism that has been used in sortilege (the drawing of lots) for centuries. Cartomancy with playing cards can be traced to at least the 1540s, predating most of the illustrated tarot decks popular today.

Playing cards are as valid a magickal tool as any other modern convenience adopted into practice. A witch who brews potions on an electric range rather than a cauldron over an open fire applies the same principle when picking up a deck of cards for divination.

The Power of Imageless Divination

One of the greatest strengths of playing cards is what they lack: prescribed imagery. Modern tarot decks feature detailed illustrations on every card, guiding (and sometimes limiting) interpretation. The Ten of Swords in the Rider-Waite-Smith deck shows a figure impaled by blades, which leaves little room for nuance. The Ten of Spades, by contrast, is simply ten spade pips. The reader must rely on intuition, psychic faculty, and personal experience to draw meaning.

This makes playing card divination closer in spirit to fire gazing (pyromancy) or crystal gazing (crystallomancy) than to illustrated tarot. The meanings are more open-ended, and interpretations can be deeply personal. A reader might find that the Three of Hearts carries a significance never mentioned in any book, one that shifts and evolves as the reader's own life changes.

A Language of Their Own

Every divination system speaks in its own dialect. Runes address different dimensions of a question than ogham symbols, and both differ from tarot. Playing cards have their own distinct voice. Many readers find that playing cards tend to speak about external events and the people surrounding the querent, while runes and tarot lean more toward internal, personal transformation.

Playing cards are a parallel system to tarot with their own strengths, history, and magickal depth.

Tarot-Numerology

Tarot-numerology combines two divinatory systems to provide quick guidance on decisions, timing, and life situations. By calculating the numerical value of a date, name, or situation, you connect that number to its corresponding Major Arcana card for insight.

Numerology assigns meanings to numbers that offer insight into your life, relationships, and the lives of the people you'll read tarot for. It commonly draws on the numbers in a birth date to calculate a Life Path or destiny number, and those same birth-date numbers can build out a full numerology chart, much like an astrology chart, offering insight into character, likely future events, and decision-making. The same techniques used for dates can also reveal the numerical vibration of a name, both yours and the names of people in your life.

Exact techniques, methods, and interpretations vary by numerology school, and any school can be paired with tarot to enrich your understanding of both the cards and the numbers themselves. Two schools are most commonly used alongside a deck: the Pythagorean and the Kabbalistic.

The Pythagorean school, also called Western numerology, traces back to the teachings of the Greek mathematician and philosopher Pythagoras. It centers on the numbers 1 through 9, applying a numerical value to each letter of the alphabet, along with the master numbers 11, 22, and 33, considered numbers of particular power and influence when present in a chart.

The Kabbalistic school is rooted in Jewish mysticism and the Kabbalah, with techniques and interpretations built on the Hebrew alphabet. Each letter carries a numerical value, and the emphasis falls more heavily on spiritual and mystical interpretation, deepening the connection between personal development, the divine, and the cosmic archetypes of the tarot.

This page uses the Pythagorean school throughout, since it's a popular and accessible starting point for weaving tarot and numerology together.

The Method

Calculate a number from a date, name, or relevant situation. Reduce multi-digit results to a single digit (except master numbers 11 and 22). Find the corresponding Major Arcana card, then interpret using both the number's meaning and the card's symbolism.

This system traditionally uses the Tarot of Marseilles, which places Justice at VIII and Strength (Force) at XI. Modern decks swap these positions. Either ordering works, but remain consistent with your chosen deck.

Calculating a Name

  1. Find the number for each letter
  2. Add all numbers together
  3. Reduce to a single digit (unless you reach 11 or 22)

Example: ROSE = 9 + 6 + 1 + 5 = 21 → 2 + 1 = 3 (The Empress)

Calculating a Date

Add all digits of the date. You can calculate two ways:

  • Month + day only gives one card
  • Month + day + year gives another card

Both calculations offer valid insight. The first focuses on the day's energy; the second incorporates the year's influence.

Example: January 15, 2026

  • Without year: 1 + 1 + 5 = 7 → Card VII (The Chariot)
  • With year: 1 + 1 + 5 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 6 = 17 → 1 + 7 = 8 → Card VIII (Justice)

Each number carries positive and negative aspects. Positive suggests alignment with that energy; negative indicates imbalance or warning.

Weaving Numerology into Your Tarot Readings

Repeating numbers or sequences within a spread can highlight specific themes or challenges. A spread dominated by cards numbered two, for example, may draw attention to relationships, partnerships, balance, and the reciprocation of energy. A rising sequence, such as the Three, Five, and Nine of Cups, signals a progression of experience and energy: if your querent is working toward a goal, this kind of build tells you their momentum is likely to continue. A cascading, or descending, sequence can instead point to regression, an unwillingness to face the future or current challenges, or something unresolved from the past that needs attention before progress becomes possible.

For readers who enjoy some on-the-spot arithmetic, try reducing the sum of every number in a reading down to a single digit to find a core number representing the reading's overall essence or theme. It can take a little time, or a calculator for larger spreads, but it's a fun way to see the main energetic thread running through a reading.

The balance of even and odd numbers across a layout is also worth a look, since it tends to set the reading's general tone. A spread weighted toward odd numbers tends to bring energy of initiative, action, and movement, while one weighted toward even numbers brings energy of balance, patience, and divine timing.

Numerology skills built this way carry over across tarot systems, so if you eventually explore the Thoth or Marseille decks, the numerical foundation you've already built will transfer directly. As your reading practice grows, so will your grasp of numerology, each reading revealing new nuances and each number taking on richer meaning over time.

Practical Applications

When to Use This Method

  • Before making important proposals or decisions
  • Considering education or career changes
  • Moving to a new home
  • Starting a new job or project
  • Major purchases or financial decisions
  • Community involvement decisions
  • Any situation requiring quick guidance

Reading the Results

  1. Note whether you land on a single digit, double digit, or master number
  2. Consult both the number meaning and the corresponding Major Arcana card
  3. Consider whether the positive or negative aspects apply to your situation
  4. If you calculated a date two ways, compare both cards for a fuller picture

The method offers quick insight without requiring a full tarot spread. Use it alongside traditional readings or as a standalone decision-making tool.

The Power of Numerology in the Minor Arcana

Numerology is vital to understanding the minor arcana. Each number from ace through ten carries a distinct vibration and message that weaves through the four suits. While the suits add their unique elemental essence to these numbers, the numerological core remains consistent. The suits show us how the core of the number is being expressed in a card, and thus experienced in your life or your querent's life. Below you'll find overviews of how numerology manifests through the minor arcana suits.

Aces

Represent beginnings and potential. They are the seed from which all growth emerges.

  • Ace of Wands: The spark of inspiration and creativity. It embodies the fire of ambition and the courage to start something new.
  • Ace of Cups: Symbolizes emotional renewal and love. It speaks of the potential for deep connection and spiritual awakening.
  • Ace of Swords: Cuts through confusion, offering clarity and truth. It signals a mental breakthrough or the beginning of an intellectual pursuit.
  • Ace of Pentacles: Represents tangible opportunities, such as financial or career prospects. It is the seed of material growth and prosperity.

Twos

Express an energy of duality and balance. It's reciprocation, exchange, and connection. Twos also signify choices and partnerships.

  • Two of Wands: Highlights planning and decision-making. It's about envisioning the future and weighing options.
  • Two of Cups: The card of partnerships, reflecting mutual respect and harmony in relationships.
  • Two of Swords: Speaks of indecision and stalemates. It reflects the challenge of balancing opposing thoughts, ideas, or mental states.
  • Two of Pentacles: Represents juggling priorities and adapting to change while maintaining equilibrium.

Threes

Represent growth and collaboration; when you add something to the balanced twos, there is an opportunity to expand. Three is also the number of creativity.

  • Three of Wands: The card of expansion and foresight, symbolizing the results of past planning and the anticipation of the future.
  • Three of Cups: Celebrates community and joy, reflecting emotional growth through shared experiences and being around like-hearted people.
  • Three of Swords: Conveys heartbreak and lessons learned through pain, a mental growth process that shapes resilience.
  • Three of Pentacles: Represents teamwork and mastery, where collaboration leads to great progress and recognition.

Fours

Bring the energy of stability and structure. It's the number of form and order, a safe place to pause.

  • Four of Wands: Celebrates stability in creativity and relationships, symbolized by milestones like weddings and achievements.
  • Four of Cups: Reflects emotional stagnation, a time of reassessment to rebuild emotional stability.
  • Four of Swords: Signals rest and recovery, emphasizing the need for mental peace and rejuvenation.
  • Four of Pentacles: Shows financial stability and security but warns against hoarding or fear of loss.

Represent conflict, challenge, and change as well as the energy of instability. It's the number that reminds us that disruption is necessary for growth.

  • Five of Wands: Represents competition, conflict, and the need to test your skills. It also emphasizes the need to find creative ways of solving problems.
  • Five of Cups: Reflects sorrow, loss, emotional hardship, and instability in the process of grieving.
  • Five of Swords: Signals conflict, often with ethical dilemmas or hollow victories.
  • Five of Pentacles: Shows financial or material challenges and a need to change sources of support.

Sixes

Represent harmony and restoration and the rejuvenation of energy after upheaval. These cards are also connected to communities.

  • Six of Wands: Celebrates victory and public recognition, symbolizing restored confidence.
  • Six of Cups: Reflects nostalgia and emotional healing, reconnecting with joy and innocence.
  • Six of Swords: Represents a journey toward mental clarity and peace, leaving turmoil behind.
  • Six of Pentacles: Signifies generosity and balance in giving and receiving, fostering material harmony.

Sevens

Signal growth, especially spiritual and personal. It's the number of introspection and overcoming challenges.

  • Seven of Wands: Speaks of defending one's position and overcoming external challenges.
  • Seven of Cups: Highlights imagination and choice, urging clarity amidst illusion.
  • Seven of Swords: Symbolizes strategy and cunning but warns of dishonesty.
  • Seven of Pentacles: Reflects patience and long-term planning, reviewing progress with an eye on future rewards.

Eights

Represent movement, momentum, and power. This is the number of mastery and application of energy.

  • Eight of Wands: Represents swift action and forward momentum, a burst of creative energy.
  • Eight of Cups: Signals emotional growth, often through leaving behind what no longer serves.
  • Eight of Swords: Reflects mental entrapment and the need for self-empowerment to break free.
  • Eight of Pentacles: Represents skill development and hard work, mastery through consistent effort.

Nines

Indicate attainment and fulfillment. This number expresses maturity and the energy of nearing completion of tasks or cycles.

  • Nine of Wands: Reflects resilience and the final push toward achievement despite challenges.
  • Nine of Cups: Symbolizes emotional satisfaction and personal happiness.
  • Nine of Swords: Reflects anxiety and mental anguish, highlighting the compounding energy being felt full force.
  • Nine of Pentacles: Represents self-sufficiency and material comfort, the rewards gained for hard work.

Tens

Represent completion, the end of a cycle, and the destination of a journey or cycle. It's the number of wholeness in the minor arcana, both positive and negative.

  • Ten of Wands: Symbolizes burdens and responsibility and work that needs completion requiring great effort.
  • Ten of Cups: Represents emotional fulfillment and harmony, the ultimate realization of love and connection.
  • Ten of Swords: Marks an ending that's often painful but necessary for new beginnings.
  • Ten of Pentacles: Reflects legacy and material abundance, the culmination of generational effort and success.

Exercise One: Tarot Deck Checklist

Before working with a physical deck alongside this book, run through this checklist to confirm it is a true tarot deck rather than a differently structured divination deck. A deck's title is not proof on its own, since some decks are labeled tarot without matching the traditional structure.

  • ☐ The deck contains seventy-eight cards total
  • ☐ Twenty-two cards carry individual titles, typically running from the Fool through the World
  • ☐ The deck is divided into four suits of fourteen cards each
  • ☐ Each suit's numbered cards run from ace through ten
  • ☐ Four court families appear across the suits, typically running from page through king, for sixteen court cards total

Meeting every point above confirms a genuine tarot deck. Many modern decks rename their cards and suits, so recognizing the underlying seventy-eight card structure matters more than the labels printed on the box.

Record which cards appeared and what they seem to communicate, working from instinct and imagery rather than turning first to a reference for the official meaning. Once each card has been considered individually, step back and look at the three-card spread as a whole, noting any theme or energy that emerges across all three.

Exercise Three: Get to Know Your Tarot Deck

This exercise centers on first impressions, whether working through a first tarot deck for the very first time or getting acquainted with a new addition to a growing collection.

Go through the deck one card at a time and sort each into three piles based on an immediate, unfiltered reaction: a pile for cards that spark a strong positive response, a pile for cards that spark a strong negative response, and a pile for cards that produce no strong feeling either way. Resist the urge to overthink any single card; the goal is a first instinct rather than a considered judgment.

Once the full deck has been sorted, reflect on each pile using the prompts below. Detailed answers are not required for every card; look instead for overall themes and patterns within each group.

Positive pile

  • Why do these cards stand out in a good way?
  • Do they share anything in common?
  • Do any reflect personal experiences or people in your life?

Negative pile

  • Why do these cards feel unappealing?
  • Do they share anything in common?
  • Do any reflect something disliked about yourself, or something feared?

Neutral pile

  • What makes these cards forgettable?
  • Is there a shared color or visual theme?
  • What changes would make them more appealing?
  • Do any still reflect personal experience despite the lack of strong reaction?

Repeating this exercise across multiple decks can be especially revealing, since a card that stands out in one deck's art style may fall flat in another.

Exercise Four: Interview Your Tarot Deck

A deck's art style, theme, and creator's intent often give it a personality of its own, one that may suit certain kinds of readings better than others. A gentler, more nostalgic deck might feel right for inner child work, while a deck with romantic artwork might lend itself naturally to relationship questions. Every deck is capable of any kind of reading, but as a collection grows, understanding each deck's particular strengths becomes useful.

This exercise uses a dedicated spread to open a conversation with a deck directly. Shuffle while holding the spread's questions in mind, cut the deck, and lay the cards out in order. Sit with initial, intuitive impressions before consulting any reference for the cards' traditional meanings.

Exercise Five: Embody the Tarot Cards

Use a deck with people in the cards for this exercise, a meditative journey into a card that puts the practitioner in a card figure's position. Those who struggle with visualizing images in the mind's eye may want to try this exercise a few times mentally first. Mirroring the figure's body language can reveal how that figure feels about its environment. If nothing surfaces that way, try physically taking on the pose or position of the figure in the card instead. Work with one figure at a time, since different energy and information tends to come through with each person on the card.

Plan for about ten minutes per tarot card used in this exercise.

Begin by selecting a physical tarot card, either at random or a favorite. This exercise works especially well with a card that feels difficult to connect with, understand, or like.

With the chosen card close by, look at it closely and memorize every detail: the colors in the foreground and background, the symbols, the stance, the clothing, and any animals. Study the card until it can be seen clearly in the mind's eye with eyes closed.

When ready, close the eyes and breathe slowly, deeply, and comfortably, feet on the ground and hands resting in the lap, palms up. On the screen of the mind, begin painting the chosen card in as much detail as possible: outline the card first, note its title, then fill in the rest of the imagery, coloring it in like paint by numbers. Open the eyes again briefly if a detail or symbol needs a second look, aiming for as clear and crisp a mental image as possible.

Once the image feels firmly in place, step into the card and take on the position of its central figure where possible, embodying their stance, facing their direction, and imagining wearing what they wear. Then look around at the surrounding environment or other figures in the card: what lies behind, in front, above, and below. Notice the weather and any animals present and how they interact with the figure. Listen for the sounds of the card and any conversations happening within it, spending as much time taking it all in as needed.

When ready to leave, begin the journey back out of the card, stepping through it and leaving behind any clothing or items picked up along the way, then bring awareness back to the physical body. Notice the sounds of the physical world and the breath, wiggle fingers and toes, and open the eyes when ready.

Before speaking with anyone else, take time to record any reflections about the card and the experience in a tarot journal. The following prompts can help guide that reflection.

  • How did it feel to take on the pose of the figure on the card?
  • What was the weather like?
  • How did the surrounding environment feel?
  • How did it feel to be inside that snapshot of the card, as though captured in a photo?
  • Was there conversation with anyone else in the card? What was said, or wanted to be said?
  • Was anyone speaking directly to you? What other sounds were present?
  • How did the card's figures, animals, and symbols interact with you?
  • What was learned about the card through the experience?

This meditation and creative visualization can be repeated any time with any card that features people.

Exercise Nine: Card a Day, One-Card Tarot Reading

For seven days, conduct a one-card tarot reading. This can happen at any point during the day or evening, though doing it first thing in the morning before the daily routine begins works especially well, since it allows time to put the reading's guidance into practice throughout the day and reflect on it come evening. Any tarot deck can be used for this exercise.

While shuffling, relax the mind and settle into a semi-meditative state, focusing on one of the suggested questions below. Once ready, cut the deck and select a card. In a tarot journal, record the card's title, the date it was pulled, and any impressions that surface before consulting a reference for its traditional meaning. Giving intuition time and space to explore the card first helps build trust in those intuitive hits. A paragraph or so of reflection is generally plenty, though how much gets written is a personal choice. The Tips for Reading and Interpreting the Cards section on the Tarot Basics & Myths page can help guide that interpretation.

Suggested questions for these one-card readings:

  • What guidance is the universe trying to provide today?
  • What do my spirit guides need me to know today?
  • What do I need to pay attention to today?
  • What do I need to avoid today?
  • How can I make the most out of today?

Exercise Eleven: Two-Card Tarot Readings

Building on one-card tarot readings, two-card tarot readings ask you to look for connections between two cards and how they relate to each other. Carry out a two-card reading daily for the next seven days, and record your interpretations in your tarot journal. Try a different two-card spread each day if you can, to help stretch your tarot-reading muscles.

When working through your interpretations, use the questions below to help extract information from the cards:

  • Are the two cards both major arcana cards?
  • Do you have two court cards?
  • Are you pulling one card frequently this week?
  • Are the cards the same number?
  • Do the numbers in the cards increase or decrease?
  • Do you get the same feeling from the pair, or are they the opposite?

Exercise Twelve: Discovering Your Major Arcana Name Card

This exercise uses numerology to connect the vibration of your full name to a Major Arcana card, offering insight into your personality, strengths, and challenges through that card's energy.

The Major Arcana isn't all sunshine and lollipops, just like life itself, and some cards read as more traditionally fortunate than others. Don't worry if your name lands on a more challenging card; it doesn't mean your life or name is doomed. Every card carries both strengths and weaknesses, and this exercise may even give you a new perspective on a card you thought you already understood.

Traditionally, this exercise uses your birth name, but if you've changed your name or go by a chosen name, feel free to use whichever name feels right, or try both and compare what each reveals about your journey and identity.

You'll need:

  • Your tarot journal and a writing instrument
  • The Major Arcana cards from your working tarot deck

Using the Letter-to-Number Chart in the Tarot-Numerology page, assign a numerical value to every letter of your full name (first, middle, and last), then add all the numbers together. Reduce that total by adding its digits together until you reach a number between 1 and 22, to align with the Major Arcana. If your number exceeds 22, keep reducing until it fits that range (for example, 25 becomes 2 + 5 = 7).

Example: MORGAN JADE FROST = (4+6+9+7+1+5) + (1+1+4+5) + (6+9+6+1+2) = 32 + 11 + 24 = 67 → 6 + 7 = 13 → 1 + 3 = 4 (The Emperor)

Once you have your final number, match it to your Major Arcana card below. No name in this exercise reduces to zero, since the Fool already exists outside and inside all of our experiences.

1–The Magician: You're resourceful and skilled with a talent for manifesting your desires into reality. You excel at using the tools at your disposal to create opportunities. This card suggests you're a natural innovator who thrives when you believe in your own power.

2–The High Priestess: You're intuitive and deeply connected to your inner wisdom. You often sense truths that others overlook and may have a natural affinity for mysticism or spirituality. This card encourages you to trust your instincts and explore the mysteries of life.

3–The Empress: You're nurturing and creative. You have a strong connection to nature and the cycles of life, often acting as a source of comfort and support for others. This card highlights your ability to create beauty and harmony in your environment.

4–The Emperor: You're a natural leader capable of providing stability and structure for those around you. You excel in situations requiring order and clear decision-making. This card reflects your strength and authority but reminds you to balance control with compassion.

5–The Hierophant: You value tradition and knowledge, often serving as a teacher or guide for others. You have a deep respect for spiritual practices and community, and you thrive in environments where you can share wisdom. This card suggests you're a seeker of truth and understanding.

6–The Lovers: You're deeply attuned to relationships and choices, often finding meaning in connections with others. This card suggests you value harmony and alignment between your actions and your heart. You may face decisions that test your commitment to your values.

7–The Chariot: You're determined and driven with a strong will to succeed. You thrive on challenges and can overcome obstacles through focus and perseverance. This card encourages you to channel your energy into clear goals and stay the course.

8–Strength: You possess inner courage and compassion, often finding calm in the face of adversity. You lead with kindness and can inspire others through your gentle strength. This card reminds you that true power lies in patience and self-control.

9–The Hermit: You're introspective and wise, seeking inner truth and deeper meaning in life. You may feel drawn to moments of solitude for reflection and growth. This card suggests you're a guide for others even as you navigate your own path.

10–Wheel of Fortune: You're attuned to the cycles of life, understanding the ebb and flow of fortune. You embrace change and adapt well to shifting circumstances. This card suggests that luck and timing play significant roles in your journey, encouraging you to trust the process.

11–Justice: You have a strong sense of fairness and accountability, often striving for balance in your life. You value truth and integrity, making decisions based on careful consideration. This card reminds you to weigh all sides before acting.

12–The Hanged Man: You have a unique ability to see situations from a different perspective. You're not afraid to pause and reflect, even if it means delaying immediate gratification. This card suggests that surrendering control can lead to profound insights.

13–Death: You're a catalyst for transformation, often embracing endings as opportunities for new beginnings. You understand that growth requires letting go of the old to make way for the new. This card highlights your resilience and ability to navigate change.

14–Temperance: You're balanced and harmonious with a talent for blending opposing forces. You excel in creating equilibrium and finding the middle path. This card suggests you bring patience and moderation to your relationships and goals.

15–The Devil: You're deeply aware of the shadows within yourself and others. You may face challenges with materialism or attachment but have the potential to break free from limiting beliefs. This card reminds you to examine what truly holds power over you.

16–The Tower: You're no stranger to upheaval, often experiencing moments of revelation that change your perspective. You have the strength to rebuild after unexpected events and grow stronger from the experience. This card highlights the importance of embracing the art of surrender.

17–The Star: You're an inspiring and hopeful individual, often radiating positivity and renewal. You have a calming presence that uplifts those around you. This card reminds you to trust in your dreams and remain optimistic about the future.

Exercise Thirteen: Find Your Birth Number and Minor Arcana Alignment

Your birth number, also known as your Life Path number or destiny number, is derived from your birth date and reveals significant insights about your personality, life purpose, and potential challenges. When you have this number, you can connect it to the numbers in the minor arcana.

The numbers in the minor arcana provide structure and movement in the deck. They represent stages of a journey, archetypes of experience, and universal principles. These energies move across the suits in the minor arcana. All the eights in the cups, swords, pentacles, and wands are an expression of that number's vibration expressed in the four suits. Learning what the numbers from ace to nine (since 10 reduces to 1) have to share with you will allow you to bring their meanings into your tarot readings.

In this exercise you'll calculate your Life Path number, identify where it sits in the progression of the minor arcana, and reflect on how it affects or reflects your life. Although there's more than one way to use your Life Path number alongside the tarot, this approach allows you to connect these modalities so you can understand your life better. If you use this exercise for your querents, it can shed light on their life paths and tarot readings as well.

You'll need:

  • Your tarot journal and writing instruments
  • The minor arcana cards from your deck

The first step is to calculate your Life Path number. Do this by following the steps below:

  1. Write down your birth date in MM/DD/YYYY format. For example, if your birth date is July 14, 1985, write: 07/14/1985.
  2. Reduce each component to a single digit:
    • Month: Reduce the month to a single digit. July is the seventh month, so it remains 7.
    • Day: Reduce the day to a single digit. For the 14th, add the digits together: 1 + 4 = 5.
    • Year: Reduce the year to a single digit. For 1985, add the digits together: 1 + 9 + 8 + 5 = 23. Then reduce 23 to a single digit: 2 + 3 = 5.
  3. Add the single digits:
    • Add the reduced month, day, and year numbers together: 7 + 5 + 5 = 17.
    • Reduce the sum to a single digit: 1 + 7 = 8. This means that 8 is your Life Path number.

Now that you have your Life Path number, take all four associated minor arcana cards out of your deck and place them in front of you. Read the information about the number and its connection to the minor arcana in the Power of Numerology in the Minor Arcana section of the Tarot-Numerology page. Take your time as you read their contents and look over the four cards in front of you.

Then take some time to reflect on your Life Path number and how its characteristics resonate with you. Using the prompts below, write about your Life Path number and your minor arcana cards.

  1. What life experiences have you had so far that connect to the minor arcana cards in front of you and the numerology of your Life Path number?
  2. What aspects of the number and cards have you embraced in your life?
  3. What aspects of the number and the cards have you denied in your life?
  4. What major lesson are you learning right now that is connected to your Life Path number and minor arcana cards?

Exercise Fourteen: Forging a Connection to the Cups

This exercise builds a personal connection to the suit of cups by exploring the symbolism of water and the feelings it stirs within you.

You'll need:

  • The cups cards from your tarot deck, from the Ace of Cups through the Ten of Cups
  • Your tarot journal and a writing instrument

Find a quiet, comfortable space free of distractions, then lay the cups cards out in front of you starting with the ace and ending with the ten, in a single row if space allows. Take a few slow breaths to settle yourself and look over the suit as a whole. Open your journal and respond to the following prompts, letting your thoughts flow without judging them.

  • What do you personally associate with the suit of cups, whether that's love, intuition, relationships, or something else?
  • How do you relate to the element of water? Does it bring up feelings of calm, strong emotion, or transformation?
  • Have you had any meaningful experiences with water, such as time spent at a reef, a waterfall, a lake, or a family swim, or another memory that comes to mind? What did that experience give you?
  • If you know your astrological natal chart, do you have several placements in the water signs (Cancer, Scorpio, Pisces)? What do you know about those signs, if anything?

Exercise Fifteen: Explore Legendary Water Vessels

Reflect on whether a particular vessel calls to you or feels connected to your own life. Consider how it relates to your understanding of the suit of cups and what emotions or thoughts it brings up, then record these reflections in your tarot journal.

Exercise Sixteen: Three-Card Tarot Readings

Three-card readings are the next step in building tarot reading skills toward larger spreads. Carry out a three-card reading daily for seven days and record interpretations in a tarot journal. Using a different three-card spread each day helps build range, and switching between multiple decks, if more than one is available, can reveal how much the reading experience shifts with a different deck.

One of the most common three-card tarot readings is the Past-Present-Future Spread. The past position reflects the choices, actions, beliefs, and situations that led to the rest of the spread, and often holds vital clues for interpreting the other two cards. The present position offers a snapshot of what is currently happening, while the future position points to what is most likely to happen next. The question asked, or the card itself, usually signals how to read that final position. For a question like "What will happen if I apply to law school in the fall?" the future position shows the most likely outcome of that path.

Preparing Your Deck

Before using a deck of playing cards for divination or spellwork, a few simple steps will transform an ordinary deck into a dedicated magickal tool.

Choosing a Deck

A brand new deck purchased specifically for divination works perfectly well, but so does one that has been sitting in a drawer for years. From a metaphysical perspective, an older deck already woven into the fabric of daily life may actually hold an advantage, since it already carries a connection to its owner.

If multiple decks are available, examine them closely before choosing. Playing cards vary more than most people realize, particularly in the court cards. Kings, Queens, and Jacks differ in posture, clothing, crown design, and the angle at which they hold their symbols. The design on the card backs also matters, as it may catch the eye and stir intuition during shuffling. No deck is inherently superior to another, but working with one that feels right strengthens the connection between reader and cards.

Removing the Jokers

The first practical step is to remove the Jokers from the deck. Despite a persistent claim that the Joker descends from the Fool card of the tarot, the two are unrelated. The Joker was invented in the United States during the 1860s for the card game Euchre, where it served as a trump card originally called the "Best Bower." The name "Joker" likely derives from the German spelling of Euchre (Juker). While both the Joker and the Fool function as trump cards in their respective games, the resemblance ends there.

Some readers choose to keep the Jokers and assign them meanings (the black Joker as the Fool, the red Joker as the Magician). This is a valid personal choice with historical precedent, since all playing cards were originally game pieces before becoming divinatory tools. However, the four suits already form a complete and well-balanced symbolic system without them.

Cleansing the Deck

Cleansing removes any residual energy the deck may carry, whether from years of card games or from the people who manufactured and packaged it. Even a new deck has passed through many hands before reaching its owner.

To cleanse a deck with salt, place the cards in a small bowl and bury them completely. Salt carries the magickal properties of purification and protection. A simple spoken intention works well during this process, something like: "Let this salt drive out any energy that does not serve my highest purpose." Leave the cards buried overnight. Working without the box allows direct contact between salt and cards for a stronger cleanse. Any stray grains caught between cards will fall out during the first few shuffles.

Consecrating the Deck

Consecration formally dedicates the deck to its new purpose as a tool for divination and magick. The method depends entirely on the practitioner's spiritual path. Norse-oriented practitioners might invoke Odin's guidance. Hellenic or Roman practitioners could petition Apollo. Wiccans may prefer to consecrate within a cast circle. The specific form matters less than the intention behind it: affirming that the work done with these cards carries purpose beyond entertainment.

Once consecrated, the deck should never be used for casual card games. If someone accidentally uses it for a round of Old Maid (which can happen, since it looks like any other deck), simply cleanse it with salt again and reconsecrate. No permanent harm is done.

Storing Your Deck

Two approaches exist, and neither is objectively better. Choose whichever resonates and stay consistent.

Sacred separation. Wrap the deck in linen or silk when not in use. Touch it only during readings or magickal work. Some readers following this approach never allow anyone else, including querents, to handle the cards. The deck remains hidden and untouched except when called upon, reinforcing its status as something set apart from mundane life.

Proximity bonding. Keep the deck close at all times. This approach draws on the magickal law of contagion: two things in sustained contact form a link between them. Having the deck nearby encourages impromptu readings and deepens the energetic bond between reader and cards. The deck becomes a constant companion rather than a reserved instrument.

Storage Options

Whichever overall approach feels right, the physical container matters too. A few reliable options:

Wooden boxes. Sturdy and long lasting, wood carries a grounding, earthy quality and doubles as a way to keep a deck out of reach of curious children or pets.

Silk wraps. Many traditions treat silk as a barrier against negative energy, making it a simple way to keep a deck's energy contained and undisturbed.

Pouches. A sewn pouch takes up little space and can be matched to a deck's color palette or theme for a personal touch.

Tins. A favorite for readers who travel with their deck, a tin keeps cards protected from damage and can often be found secondhand for character as well as function.

Whatever the choice, the deck should stay somewhere dry, safe, and easy to reach. A tool left buried under other belongings does little good when a reading is needed on short notice.

Cleansing and Charging Ritual

Even a well cared for deck can start to feel energetically heavy, or its messages may seem harder to read clearly than usual. When this happens, it helps to consider three things: personal energy, the energy of the reading space, and the energy of the deck itself. Readers who are especially sensitive to energy may benefit from a regular practice of clearing their space in addition to their cards.

A cleansing and charging ritual does not need to be elaborate to be effective, and a simple routine is easier to maintain consistently. A few approachable methods:

Resetting the order. Sorting the deck back into its original sequence resets it both physically and symbolically.

Moonlight. Leaving the deck on a windowsill during a full moon lets its light recharge the cards; the full moon occurs roughly thirteen times a year, offering regular opportunities for this practice.

Smoke. Passing the deck through the smoke of herbs such as sage, palo santo, or lavender is believed to clear away stagnant energy. Always research any plant material before burning it, and ventilate the space well.

Salt and herbs. Resting the deck in a shallow dish of rock salt and cleansing herbs can draw out unwanted energy while also reconsecrating the cards.

Crystals. Storing a deck alongside stones such as Citrine, Smoky Quartz, Black Tourmaline, or Amethyst is thought to support positivity, protection, and intuitive clarity, respectively.

Sound. Singing bowls, bells, or drums can be used to clear a deck's energy through vibration.

None of these practices are required. Some readers maintain an intentional ritual every time they use their deck, while others never reorder their cards at all. Either approach is valid as long as it fits the reader's own style.

The Language of Colors in the Tarot

The colors used in tarot are often carefully considered during a deck's creation, true for the Rider-Waite-Smith tarot as well as most decks available on the market. Some decks select a color scheme for each suit that aligns with that element's core energies, while other creators favor specific palettes such as pastels or vibrant neon. Colors convey messages through vibration and through the meanings assigned to them by cultures worldwide.

Common interpretations of color vary depending on cultural background, making it worthwhile to add personal meaning to the ones offered here. Some colors or palettes may simply never resonate, no matter how much effort goes into connecting with them. The interpretations below serve as a starting point for developing personal meanings for the colors found in tarot.

Black

Black holds the absence of light, signifying emptiness, loss, mystery, and depression. It also proves essential for every other color to carry depth and variation of hue, making it a forceful feature that represents formality, dignity, force, convention, stability, and zero tolerance. Black connects as well to protection against negativity.

Blue

Blue stands as a dominant color found throughout nature, visible in the sky and the ocean alike. Its meanings include open spaces, freedom, imagination, expansiveness, inspiration, peace, and sensitivity, leaving behind a sense of calm and trust. Blue connects to the throat chakra, and its negative traits surface through challenging emotions, stagnant waters, and predictable behavior.

Brown

Brown carries the energy of groundedness and nature, the feeling familiar to anyone who has squished their toes into rich, moist earth. This earthy color reads as tangible, practical, stable, nurturing, and solid, without frills and strongly conservative in nature, offering exactly what it appears to be. Brown also represents decay and organic matter breaking down.

Gray

Gray brings uncertainty, its message clear whenever fog rolls in and its haze settles: distortion, neutrality, uniformity, intensity, and austerity. It signals a need for establishing middle ground, along with a reminder that things are sometimes different than they first appear. This color calls for a pause before acting.

Green

Green stands as a lucky color associated with all things that grow, its lush arrival each spring bringing attributes of youth, sentimentality, nature, adventure, growth, and health. Green connects to the heart chakra, and though usually harmonious, its negative traits surface through envy, materialism, and jealousy, fitting given money's own bright green color. This bright, happy color can also turn irresponsible and unstable.

Indigo

Indigo represents the unknown depths of the sea alongside emotion, strength, fluidity, persuasiveness, expressiveness, and pervasiveness. Connected to the third eye chakra, this energetic color carries less positive traits through theatrics and criticism, while holding the capacity to both trigger and inspire.

Orange

Orange forms a subdued blend of aggressive red and high pitched yellow, carrying warmth and glow without red's hot intensity. This color speaks to harmony, aspiration, sociability, courage, and contentment, and connects to the sacral chakra. Orange also reads as brash, driven, intelligent, and ambitious.

Red

Red exudes physical energy and intensity, implying a practical approach paired with movement. This color evokes strength, courage, passion, aggression, sexuality, and vibrancy, which explains why so many of the world's biggest brands choose a red logo. Red connects to the root chakra, and its burning intensity can quickly fan out of control, serving as a warning of impending danger and intense emotions such as anger.

Violet

Violet carries one of the highest energies in the color spectrum, speaking of deep spirituality, wisdom, and devotion, and often connecting to spiritual leaders and teachers. Found in the hue of flowers and sleepy sunsets, violet evokes communion, grandeur, high ideals, ambition, and peace. This color connects to the crown chakra and can read as both mysterious and arrogant.

White

White stands as the color of possibilities, representing peace, cleansing, illumination, purity, innocence, and the highest level of understanding. Some tarot decks use white to represent negative space within a card.

Yellow

Yellow carries a high vibration, just like the bright, warm rays of the sun. This color radiates creativity, protection, intellect, positivity, and clarity, bright and cheerful enough to serve as an instant mood lifter. Yellow connects to the solar plexus chakra.

Keeping a Tarot Journal

A tarot journal tracks how a reader's relationship with the cards and their deck changes over time. Because a single card can reveal new layers of meaning between one reading and the next, keeping a written record surfaces patterns and recurring lessons that would otherwise go unnoticed.

Why Keep One

Describing a card's artwork and the feelings it brings up trains intuition and builds familiarity with the deck. A journal also creates a reference to revisit later, so a reader can measure how accurate a reading turned out to be and notice where a question could have been phrased more clearly. Both newcomers and experienced professionals benefit from this practice, since writing through symbols and possible meanings reinforces what has been learned.

Beyond formal readings, a journal is also a place to note intuitive impressions tied to the tarot, such as thoughts that surface during meditation with the cards, dream imagery connected to a specific card, or an unrelated moment that suddenly calls a card to mind.

Common Obstacles

Reluctance to begin usually traces back to a handful of concerns: disliking one's own handwriting, feeling short on time, or not wanting to mark up an appealing notebook. Each has a workaround. Drawing or typing can stand in for handwriting, short recordings can stand in for written entries, and any tool eventually earns its keep simply by being used. A practice picked up in bursts, set aside for weeks, then returned to, still counts as progress. Consistency matters less than continuing to show up for it.

Choosing a Format

There is no single correct format, only one that gets used: a fresh notebook, a well worn binder already on hand, or a digital option such as a blog or voice log. Above all, a tarot journal is a private space intended purely to support a reader's own exploration and growth, with no expectation that anyone else will ever see it.
