History of Playing Cards

Playing cards have traveled across continents and centuries, evolving from Chinese woodblock prints into the familiar deck of 52 cards used worldwide today.

Origins in China

The earliest known playing cards appeared during the Tang Dynasty in China, created sometime in the 800s using woodblock printing. These first decks lacked the suits and numbered sequences we recognize today, but they established the fundamental concept of a portable set of printed cards used for games and, likely, for fortune-telling.

Westward Through Persia and Egypt

As cards migrated along trade routes through Persia and into the Mamluk Sultanate (which governed Egypt and parts of western Arabia from the 1200s to the 1500s), they evolved considerably. The Egyptian Mamluk deck featured four suits, twelve pip cards, and three court cards per suit, a structure remarkably close to modern playing cards. The court cards displayed abstract geometric designs rather than human figures, likely reflecting Islamic restrictions on depicting sentient beings.

Arrival in Europe

Playing cards entered Europe in the 1300s, probably through Mamluk trade connections. The first European decks carried suits of Coins, Cups, Polo-Sticks, and Swords. Since polo was largely unknown in Europe at the time, Polo-Sticks quickly became Clubs or Cudgels.

From there, suit symbols continued to evolve along regional lines. Three broad categories emerged:

  • French: Diamonds, Hearts, Clubs, Spades (used in the UK and US today)
  • Latin: Coins, Cups, Clubs/Batons, Swords (used in Italy and Spain)
  • Germanic: Regional variations with distinct imagery

Birth of the Tarot

In the mid-1400s, card makers in northern Italian cities added a "trump" suit of twenty-two illustrated cards to Latin-style decks. These expanded decks were called carte da trionfi (triumph cards), known today as tarot. The oldest surviving examples were painted for the Visconti-Sforza family, rulers of Milan. Like standard playing cards, these decks were originally used for card games, not divination.

The trump cards featured elaborate imagery rooted in Roman Catholic symbolism, depicting figures like the Pope, the Devil, and Judgment Day. This religious connection was likely strategic, since card games were frequently condemned by both Church and secular authorities. Cards were sometimes called "the devil's picture book."

Cartomancy and Sortilege

Despite official disapproval, card games persisted as popular entertainment. Both playing cards and tarot were almost certainly used for divination alongside gaming. This practice, called cartomancy, belongs to a broader category of divination known as sortilege: the drawing of lots. Sortilege encompasses divination with dice, runes, and any closed set of symbols drawn at random and interpreted. Playing card divination can be documented as far back as 1540.

The Mystical Turn

Tarot began to take on overt mystical significance in the eighteenth century, when a French Protestant minister named Antoine Court speculated that the tarot derived from the Egyptian Book of Thoth. He also linked the twenty-two trump cards to the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. These ideas generated fresh interest in tarot as a spiritual system, though the non-trump suits still looked much like ordinary playing cards, with an Eight of Swords being simply a picture of eight swords.

The Rider-Waite-Smith Revolution

The pivotal shift came in 1909, when occultist Arthur Edward Waite commissioned artist Pamela Colman Smith to illustrate all 78 cards of a tarot deck. Both were members of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. Smith created descriptive scenes for every card, not just the trumps, giving readers visual cues for interpretation. The deck, published by William Rider & Son in 1910, replaced overt Christian imagery with broader mystical symbolism (the Pope became the Hierophant, the Papess became the High Priestess).

This illustrated approach gave the Rider-Waite-Smith deck a practical advantage over both playing cards and earlier tarot decks. If a reader forgot the meaning of the Ten of Swords, the image of a figure impaled on the ground made the general interpretation obvious. Over time, tarot became the dominant tool for card divination.

Playing Cards Endure

Despite tarot's rise, playing cards never lost their place in the cartomancer's toolkit. Their long history, accessibility, and the unique quality of imageless divination continue to make them a powerful and legitimate system for magickal practice.

Reading Playing Cards

Learning to interpret fifty-two cards without illustrated imagery can feel overwhelming. Rune readers only need to master sixteen to thirty-three symbols, and ogham practitioners work with twenty-five. A full deck of playing cards nearly doubles that count. Fortunately, a simple framework built on elemental theory and numerology reduces the task dramatically.

The Element-Number Framework

Rather than memorizing each card individually, learn thirteen core symbols: four elements (one per suit) and nine numbers (Ace through Nine, with Ten as a completion). Combining these two layers produces the meaning of any pip card in the deck.

The four suits correspond to the classical elements:

  • Hearts: Water. Emotion.
  • Clubs: Fire. Transformation.
  • Diamonds: Earth. Fortune.
  • Spades: Air. Movement.

Each number carries its own energy that blends with the suit's element. The Four of Hearts, for example, combines the stability of the number four with the emotional nature of Water, producing a meaning rooted in secure relationships and friendship. This pattern holds across all pip cards from Ace through Ten.

Court Cards

The element-number shortcut does not extend to court cards (Jack, Queen, King). These cards carry their own meanings tied to personality types and roles. However, the elemental influence of the suit still applies. A Queen of Spades carries the Air element's sharpness and intellectual edge, while a Jack of Hearts channels Water's emotional depth.

Meaning Lives in the Reader

The cards themselves are printed paper. Interpretation comes from within the reader, who uses the cards to activate psychic and intuitive faculties. Published meanings provide a foundation, but every reader develops personal associations over time. A particular card might come to represent a specific person, a recurring situation, or a private symbol. These personal layers shift and evolve as the reader's own life changes.

Context Changes Everything

No card exists in isolation. A skilled reader examines the entire layout before focusing on any single card. Surrounding cards can reinforce, modify, or completely reverse a card's meaning.

Consider the Four of Hearts again. In a layout dominated by harmony and contentment, it confirms emotional stability. But if the surrounding cards point to chaos and upheaval, that same Four of Hearts shifts from announcing stability to advising the querent to seek it. The card becomes a call to remain calm rather than a statement of present conditions.

This mutable quality applies to every card in the deck. Each card functions as a symbol shaped by its neighbors, the question at hand, and the reader's intuition.

Building Fluency

The element-number framework provides the foundation. Once the associations between elements and numbers become instinctive, personal experience layers additional meaning onto each card over time.

Preparing for a Reading

Before drawing cards, focus the mind. This can be accomplished through a short meditation or simply by concentrating on breathing for a minute or two. Inhale to the count of four, hold for an equal count, then release slowly to a final count of four. Repeat until a sense of relaxation flows through the body.

Alternatively, some readers prepare through prayer. The prayer should reflect the reader's own spirituality. A reader who follows a single deity will naturally pray to that deity for guidance. Those on a polytheistic path may wish to direct prayer to a deity associated with prophecy or magick, though the connection with the deity matters more than the deity's traditional domain. A simple invocation such as "(Name of deity), I ask for your guidance" is sufficient. Offerings of wine, mead, or incense may accompany the prayer, though they can also be given afterward if they would distract from the reading. Prayer can be reserved for more significant readings; a quick daily draw does not usually require formal invocation.

Shuffling and Cutting the Deck

The act of shuffling serves a dual purpose: it randomizes the cards and prepares the reader mentally. While shuffling, set aside extraneous thoughts. If focusing on breathing helps, do that while shuffling. Continue for as long as it takes to feel centered and ready.

When reading for someone else, the reader shuffles first, then passes the deck to the querent. This connects the querent with the cards through the law of contagion, a magickal principle stating that any two things that come into contact remain connected after they are separated. The same principle is why spellcasters seek personal items belonging to the person they are working magick for. The querent should shuffle for as long as they need. Do not rush them or judge the length of their shuffle.

After shuffling is complete, the querent (or the reader, if reading for themselves) cuts the deck into three equal parts using the left hand. The left hand is used because it symbolically represents the receptive, psychic hand. Three parts are used because three is the number of creativity and expression, symbolically asking the cards to express the pattern of the unfolding universe. Then, using the left hand, reassemble the deck by placing the middle part on the top part and both of these on the bottom part. This final step is a symbolic transition between preparation and the actual drawing of the cards.

Shuffling and Selecting Cards

Many people worry about shuffling incorrectly, but the message comes through regardless of technique or polish. Even experienced readers occasionally send cards flying across the room. Practice builds confidence over time, and the methods below offer a starting point.

Shuffling Techniques

The riffle shuffle. Split the deck in half, angle the corners toward each other, and let the cards fall together in an interlocking pattern. This method can wear cards down over time, so it suits sturdier decks better than a treasured one meant to stay pristine. It works especially well with oversized, square, or round decks, and can look impressive once mastered.

Over and under shuffling. Hold the deck in the nondominant hand and transfer cards from back to front, or the reverse, with the dominant hand. This familiar method suits standard sized decks well.

The washing machine technique. Spread the cards face down across a table and mix them by hand. This relaxed approach works well for smaller hands or unusually shaped decks and doubles as a way to infuse personal energy into the cards.

The piles technique. Divide the deck into a random number of small piles, then gather them back together. More piles mean a more thorough shuffle, making this method helpful for anyone still building confidence in their shuffling.

Shuffling machines. For anyone who struggles to shuffle by hand, such as due to arthritis, a shuffling machine offers a practical alternative. Most machines on the market are built for playing card sized decks, though tarot decks in that size are available.

Selecting Cards for a Reading

Once the deck is shuffled, the next step is choosing which cards to use. As with shuffling, there is no single correct approach. Some readers prefer not to let others touch their cards, while others invite the querent to select their own. Remote readings require the reader to lay the cards out alone. Whatever the arrangement, the right cards tend to find their way into the reading regardless of who selects them. The number of cards drawn depends on the spread chosen or the reader's intuition, decided before the shuffle begins.

Fan, scan, and pick. After shuffling, fan the cards out for the querent. In person, the querent can run a palm across the fan and pull whichever cards call to them, either by feel or by sight. In a remote reading, the reader can run a palm across the cards while the querent calls out when to stop, and that becomes the chosen card. This process repeats once for each position in the spread, with the cards laid out in the order selected.

Pick a pile. After shuffling, cut the deck into piles, most commonly three, and ask the querent which pile draws their attention. The reading is then laid out from that pile. If the reader is comfortable with their deck being handled, the querent can shuffle and divide the piles directly.

Selecting by image. This method skips shuffling entirely. The querent views the card images and chooses based on directed prompts, which works particularly well for counseling or healing focused sessions where resonance matters more than randomness.

Roll the dice. After shuffling and setting an intention, roll a die and count through the deck to the corresponding card. Dice with more than six sides, such as a twelve sided or twenty sided die, work best for this playful, chance driven method.

Shuffling and selecting cards is ultimately a personal art. Whether following these methods exactly or adapting them, the intention behind each action matters more than the technique itself.

Playing Cards for Ancestor Divination

Playing cards can be dedicated to communing with ancestors and used as a simple, powerful yes-or-no divination system. This page covers the three-card draw method, how to phrase questions well, how to use divination to assess offerings, and the key caveats for working responsibly with this system.

The Three-Card Draw

When asking a yes-or-no question, draw three cards. Red suits (Hearts and Diamonds) are read as positive omens. Black suits (Clubs and Spades) are read as negative omens.

ResultReading
🔴🔴⚫ Two red, one blackWeak yes. The outcome may be attained, but stay alert. Additional work may be needed.
⚫⚫⚫ Three blackStrong no. A cleansing to reset your energy field is recommended after this response.

Always end a session on a yes. If you receive a weak or strong no, continue asking questions about how to improve your circumstance through prayer, offerings, or practical action until you receive a yes.

This method works with any binary system beyond playing cards, including flipping a coin. Advanced readers may add nuance to the yes/no by further interpreting each card according to their full cartomantic system.

Phrasing Questions

The most important skill in structured yes/no divination is phrasing the question correctly:

  • The answer must be yes or no.
  • The "yes" must be the positive outcome.

Example: Asking "Will my boss fire me?" and pulling three black cards gives you a no, which sounds good, but the energy is overwhelmingly negative. Rephrase so the desired answer is yes: "Will I keep my job?"

The No Loop

Sometimes every question returns a no, no matter what is asked. This may indicate unseen forces at work. Consult a professional diviner. A useful short-circuit question: "Should I consult a professional diviner about this?"

Avoid "Should" Questions

Some diviners refuse questions that begin with "should" (e.g., "Should I quit my job?"). These questions often mask a desire to hand off responsibility for a decision, or a wish to know how to avoid pain. Pain is an inevitable part of life, and ancestors, who no longer experience pain or pleasure, are not well-positioned to advise on avoiding it.

Ask questions that help you make decisions with greater confidence, not questions that make decisions for you. Use divination when you are blocked, confused, or partially perceiving something and need confirmation or more detail. Divination is medicine.

Divining for Offerings

The three-card draw can also be used to ask ancestors whether they desire specific offerings.

Example question: "Would you like a slice of red velvet cake as an offering, in exchange for helping me attract good people to go out with?"

ResultReading
🔴🔴⚫ Two red, one blackWeak yes. The offering can be given, but other things would build better communion.
⚫⚫⚫ Three blackStrong no. The offering must not be given; the idea to ask may have come from the wrong motivations.

You are never forced to give ancestors what they request. But receiving a strong yes and ignoring it may feel discourteous. Start with simple, low-cost offerings and escalate gradually:

  1. More of what you've already given (more incense, another candle)
  2. Something you haven't given but already have on hand (food or liquor from the pantry)
  3. Something cheap and easy to acquire (flowers from a nearby shop)
  4. Something moderately expensive or harder to find (a specific liquor; a party in their honor)
  5. Something extra (a tool, a statue, a pilgrimage)

Caveats

1. Know Who You're Talking To

Before relying on this system, be confident you are actually talking to your ancestors and not another spirit or random noise. This confidence grows over time. Once you have kept an ancestor altar for a while, notice the energy it carries: how your body feels, what genre of thoughts arise. Check whether that same energy is present during divination, or whether something feels different.

2. Don't Ask Dumb Questions

Don't ask questions you already know the answer to. Don't ask about inconsequential things. If you are agnostic or skeptical about divination, that may be a sign to wait. Don't ask questions as tests. It erodes trust on both sides of the relationship.

3. Don't Let Divination Run Your Life

You are the ancestor who is alive right now. You hold the responsibility and privilege to make decisions. Divination is a tool to help you make them better, not a mechanism for avoiding them.

Dedicating a Deck

To establish a stronger bond, consider dedicating a specific deck of cards solely to ancestral communication rather than using a general-purpose deck. One traditional method: cleanse a new deck with benzoin at the new moon, then wrap it with a piece of black tourmaline in silk. Keep it on your ancestor altar.

Creating Your Own Tarot Spreads

Designing your own tarot spreads gives you clear, focused readings tailored to whatever question or situation is at hand, rather than trying to force a borrowed spread to fit. An existing spread, including any of the ones already documented here, can also be adapted to better suit a specific circumstance if starting from a foundation feels more comfortable than building from scratch. Some readers love creating original spreads, while others are perfectly happy relying on the thousands already available.

When designing an original spread, a few key factors keep it practical, meaningful, and aligned with its purpose.

Be Clear and Intentional

Define the spread's purpose before starting to design it. A spread can be built around something very specific or something broad. Getting clear on the question or issue being explored, and the outcome the reading is meant to support, comes first.

The Number of Cards

A three card spread can carry just as much power as a fifteen card one. Too many cards too quickly can become overwhelming, so experimenting with different counts and positions helps find the right balance. A complex issue may call for more cards to explore different angles, while a simpler question often only needs two or three.

Relevant Position Assignment

Each position should carry a meaning tied directly to the question being explored, so the positions work together toward a clear answer. Like a well told story, a spread benefits from a satisfying, connected structure from start to finish, giving the querent both an answer and something empowering to act on. A spread that only surfaces challenges without also reflecting strengths and blessings misses a chance to bring balance to the reading. When assigning meaning to each position, it helps to ask whether the spread itself would feel worth using, then refine from there.

Test Run Your Spreads

Once a first draft exists, put it to use. Shuffle the deck and see how the spread performs in practice, staying open to adjustments if certain positions fall flat or fail to produce useful insight. Refining a spread through testing is part of building real experience as a reader, and preferences around style will keep evolving with practice.

Example: Creating a Spiritual Growth Spread

Here is one way a spread focused on spiritual growth might come together:

  1. Intention: Understand the current state of one's spiritual self and identify areas for further development.
  2. Number of cards: Five cards, one for each growth area: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, challenges, and potential outcomes.
  3. Positions and assigned meanings:
    • Card 1, Strengths: the spiritual strengths currently present.
    • Card 2, Weaknesses: the weaknesses that may be slowing spiritual growth.
    • Card 3, Opportunities: the opportunities available for spiritual development.
    • Card 4, Challenges: the challenges that need to be overcome to grow.
    • Card 5, Potential Outcome: the most likely outcome if this reading is put into practice.
  4. Layout: The cards could be arranged in a star pattern, with strengths at the top, weaknesses and opportunities on either side, challenges at the bottom, and the potential outcome in the center.
  5. Testing: Use the spread for an actual reading, reflect on how each position resonates with the current situation, and adjust positions or meanings as needed.

The Court Cards

The court cards in tarot typically represent people, personalities, and different aspects of the self. Understanding these cards deepens tarot practice significantly, since they reveal relationship dynamics, the influence of other people, and the many roles played throughout life.

Many readers treat the court cards as the minor arcana's personification of the energy and rank carried by each suit. They can represent people in someone's life, an aspect of the self, or the characteristics needed to handle a particular situation, and their meaning shifts more fluidly depending on the reading's context and the surrounding cards.

Although the exact ranking labels differ across modern decks, the order from least to most powerful stays consistent, tracking a kind of growth through experience and the maturing of mind, body, and spirit.

Pages

Pages sit at the start of the court card journey, carrying youthful, inquisitive energy and representing the earliest stages of a new path. They embody curiosity, potential, and the initial stirrings of new experience, acting as messengers and initiators who signal the start of exploration, learning, and discovery. Each page carries a distinct flavor tied to its element: emotional sensitivity for the Page of Cups, intellectual curiosity for the Page of Swords, passionate enthusiasm for the Page of Wands, and practical diligence for the Page of Pentacles. Together, the pages point toward approaching life with an open mind, a willingness to grow, and excitement for new beginnings.

Knights

Knights represent action, movement, and the active pursuit of goals, carrying the dynamic, sometimes turbulent energy of taking initiative and pushing forward. Each knight channels its suit's questing spirit into the world: the emotional, romantic journey of the Knight of Cups, the intellectual, communicative drive of the Knight of Swords, the passionate, adventurous energy of the Knight of Wands, and the methodical, determined progress of the Knight of Pentacles. Together, the knights mark the shift from planning into action, encouraging active engagement with life, a willingness to take risks, and the courage to face challenges directly. They stand as a reminder that growth often comes through lived experience, obstacles included.

Queens

Queens embody maturity, inner strength, and the nurturing side of their element. As the emotional, intellectual, creative, and material rulers of their suits, they represent the deep understanding and mastery that comes from experience and reflection. Each queen channels her suit's energy with grace and authority: intuitive compassion for the Queen of Cups, sharp intellect and clear communication for the Queen of Swords, fiery creativity and confident leadership for the Queen of Wands, and practical wisdom and nurturing care for the Queen of Pentacles. Together, the queens balance power with sensitivity, showing that real leadership can be rooted in empathy and inner truth as much as authority.

Kings

Kings represent authority, mastery, and the culmination of energy within their suit, embodying the peak of power, responsibility, and control. Each king exercises influence built from the knowledge and experience gained along his journey: emotional maturity and compassionate leadership for the King of Cups, intellectual clarity and strategic decisiveness for the King of Swords, dynamic leadership and visionary creativity for the King of Wands, and stable, practical stewardship for the King of Pentacles. Together, the kings represent self-mastery and the responsibility that comes with it, showing that true leadership involves both guiding external circumstances and mastering the self.

Multiple Court Cards in a Reading

When several court cards appear together in a reading, interpersonal dynamics take center stage. This can point to friction with the people involved, signal that many people are connected to the situation, or reflect the outcome of a decision that will affect a wider group.

Number: 4. Keyword: stability.

Fours are steady and reliable, sometimes to the point of stubbornness. They express their suit's elemental influence with more emphasis than Threes and in a way that is less mutable. Changing the influence of a Four can be difficult, though that same stubborn stability becomes a blessing when the card indicates something worth keeping.

Fours carry a low-key energy rather than anything fiery or erratic. The Four of Hearts speaks of emotional relationships, but these are the stable emotions of friendship or the calm, steady affection of a long-term partnership rather than the heady feelings of new romance. Because of the endurance of the number four, the naturally stable suits (Diamonds and Hearts) are especially positive under this influence. The situation indicated by a Four will remain the same unless the querent takes active and persistent steps to create change.

The Four of Hearts brings constancy to the querent's emotional relationships. It can sometimes relate to romance, but only indirectly. If the querent has been dating someone for a while, this card could indicate that the other person is ready to settle into something more permanent.

More often, though, this card speaks of friendly, nonromantic relationships. It can involve the querent's social circle, workplace connections, or family bonds. Like the Four of Diamonds, it is almost always positive.

This is a good card even for introverts, because the relationships it describes are unlikely to be overwhelming. They are low-key but fulfilling. The only disappointment would come if the querent is hoping for something wild and passionate, as the Four of Hearts points to steady warmth rather than fiery intensity.

Court cards, also called face cards, depict human faces. Though influenced by elemental associations like the rest of the deck, court cards almost always represent people who can influence the querent directly through their actions and decisions. The elemental influence of the suit shapes the personality and energy of the person the card represents.

Jacks represent younger, less mature people regardless of gender or archetypal role. These are individuals who influence the querent, so a Jack rarely indicates a child unless it is the querent's own adult child.

For querents over forty, Jacks usually point to younger people. Otherwise, a Jack might indicate someone the querent's own age but less experienced. For very young querents in their early teens, a Jack could even represent an actual child.

Further distinctions are a matter of perspective and vary from one reading to another. It is up to the reader to determine how a court card should be interpreted based on who they are and who they are reading for.

The suit of Hearts breaks the typical age rule for court cards. The Jack of Hearts can represent a person of any age. The defining quality is that this person has been in the querent's life for a while, not someone new or yet to be met.

This person shares a significant emotional relationship with the querent. The connection is not always romantic; it could be a lover or spouse, but just as easily a family member, longtime friend, or coworker. There is always an emotional bond of some kind. The Jack of Hearts would not indicate a mere neighbor or acquaintance unless there is a genuine emotional involvement between them.

Whatever the nature of the relationship, the Jack of Hearts represents someone with whom the querent has a positive, meaningful rapport.

In numerology, multi-digit numbers are reduced to a single digit by adding their digits together. The number 10 (1 + 0) reduces to 1, creating similarities between the Tens and the Aces. Like the Aces, the Tens are aggressive cards that express their suit's elemental influence explicitly.

The difference is that Tens lack the triumphant quality of Aces. Aces hold the highest value in card games, while Tens are trumped by Aces and all three court cards. A Ten is always forceful but not necessarily triumphant for the querent. The Ten of Hearts and Ten of Diamonds are both excellent cards to see in a reading. Surrounding cards help clarify how the situation will affect the querent.

In Readings

The Ten of Hearts indicates strong, overwhelming emotional attraction, which may or may not be welcome. In the right circumstances, this is a wonderful card. It represents complete fulfillment, a level of joy so intense it catches the breath. This card predicts the kind of rush of emotion that can affect every thought.

Usually the Ten of Hearts is positive, but its sheer force can sometimes lead to undesirable outcomes. In romance, its intensity can actually sabotage a relationship by overwhelming the other person. It can also warn that intense emotions will become a distraction. If the querent can remain in control of their thoughts and actions, they can expect an exhilarating emotional ride.

The emotions expressed by this card are not necessarily romantic or sensual. An ecstatic spiritual experience can be just as powerful. The Ten of Hearts often speaks of romance, but it can indicate any kind of deep emotion. At its core, it is the sense of complete emotional fulfillment.

What a Coven Is

A coven is a group of practitioners who gather regularly for shared magickal work. The word derives from the Latin conventus, meaning a gathering or assembly, the same root that gives us convent, convention, covenant, and convene.

Covens range from the strictly religious to the entirely practical. Some concentrate on healing. Others specialize in necromancy, divination, or the invocation of deities. Some devote themselves to political workings, directing collective power at those in positions of public authority. Others pursue knowledge and power as an end in itself. Many celebrate the eight Sabbats as their primary collective activity, treating the gatherings as occasions of genuine festivity rather than solemn ceremony.

Solo Practice vs. Coven Work

A solo working requires only privacy and a modest degree of soundproofing, the latter serving less as a precaution against noise complaints and more as an aid to the uninhibited release of emotional energy, which is of primary importance in all magickal work. Any corner of a private home is sufficient for solo practice.

Coven work requires a larger space and a compatible group, but the advantages are considerable. A magickal operation performed by a well-aligned group will often succeed spectacularly where a solo effort achieves only moderate success. The principle is straightforward: strength multiplies with numbers when the emotional rapport and shared purpose are genuine.

The Coven Entity

One of the central ideas of coven practice is that a well-sustained group does not merely add individual powers together. If sufficient pyramid power is brought to it and held in place by genuine emotional rapport, practitioners believe that a pool or vortex of collective energy begins to form.

This vortex, sustained by regular ritual, eventually becomes two things at once: an energy bank from which all members can draw to supplement their personal resources, and an artificially constructed collective deep mind, independent in its own right.

This is the magickal rationale behind the secrecy required in most serious occult groups. The rituals and symbols particular to the group, called triggering devices, are kept from outsiders not out of fear of misuse, but because interference by the uninitiated, particularly those of a hostile or sceptical disposition, undermines and disperses all the work invested in building the entity.

Cowans

The uninitiated are traditionally referred to as cowans. The word has roots in Freemasonry, where it originally referred to a stoneworker without formal guild training. In the context of witchcraft, a cowan is simply anyone who has not been brought into the working group, and whose presence risks destabilizing its established energetic structure.

Size and Membership

By tradition, a coven is limited to thirteen members, inclusive of its leaders. The number corresponds to the thirteen full moons of the lunar year and is also, practically speaking, the largest number of people who can work comfortably within a nine-foot circle.

When membership exceeds thirteen, a new coven splits away from the original one. Traditional territory is observed, with at least three miles maintained between the meeting places of distinct covens. This custom combines older notions of covendom, the territorial sphere of a coven's influence, with the pragmatic caution of the persecution era, when small, dispersed groups were simply safer.

In goddess-oriented covens with an emphasis on the sexual aspects of the Craft, membership is ideally composed of six male-female couples plus a leader, making thirteen total. These traditions also require that initiation be conferred from sex to sex (man upon woman and vice versa), with an exception made for parent and child. This rule does not apply in all branches of the Craft.

Esbats and Sabbats

Covens meet informally at gatherings called Esbats, a word derived from the French for "to frolic," reflecting the historically unsolemn, celebratory character of a witches' meeting.

The eight annual Sabbats mark the turning of the seasons and the ebb and flow of elemental tides. In addition to their magickal significance, they have always been occasions of genuine festivity. A coven that treats Sabbats as purely ritualistic obligations misses the point. Sabbats are a time of renewal of friendship and elemental power, and a time of enjoyment.

Requirements for a Functioning Coven

Two conditions are essential:

  1. Members must be like-minded: sympathetic to one another in basic belief and genuinely in emotional rapport.
  2. Members must bring sufficient magickal dedication and intensity of purpose, understood not as fanaticism but as the ability to focus the mind on a problem and release the imagination within appropriate limits.

All members should be fully and practically conversant with the four powers of the Witches' Pyramid. The more magickally developed the individuals, the more potent the coven as a collective entity.

The Seven Points of Forming a Coven

The practical establishment of a coven can be organized under seven headings:

  1. The Nature of Your Coven: the coven's identifying symbols, totems, and general symbolic framework.
  2. Coven Hierarchy: whether or not leaders and degrees of initiation exist, and how they are structured.
  3. Initiation Ritual: one or more rituals using coven symbolism, corresponding to any hierarchy established.
  4. A Binding Oath of Secrecy: imposed upon all members at admission, reinforced by the magickal weight of surrendered object links such as a drop of blood or a lock of hair.
  5. Coven Name: a magickal name taken specifically for coven work, which may be the same as or in addition to any name assumed for solo practice.
  6. Witch Insignia: the physical marker of membership worn by all members: pendant, ring, bracelet, necklace, garter, or similar.
  7. Coven Sabbat Rituals: workings designed for performance at one or more of the eight Sabbats, drawing heavily on the established coven symbolism.

The Nature of Your Coven

The symbolism chosen to represent a coven's orientation should draw from the mythological and magickal tradition the group wishes to align with. Tradition-minded practitioners generally recommend restricting this to European sources, keeping the group in contact with the Western magickal tradition. Others follow Dion Fortune's maxim that all gods are one God, all goddesses are one Goddess, and there is one Initiator, which permits a nonsectarian, broadly inclusive approach.

The source material chosen for coven symbolism should reflect the group's primary orientation:

  • Knowledge and sky power: symbols associated with Herne and the sky powers in all their forms
  • Power and fire: symbols consonant with the Horned One as Lord of Fire and Energy
  • Healing: imagery connected with Mother Hertha
  • Love: orientation toward the Lady Habondia

The coven emblem, or logo, should be designed like a heraldic crest: a single composite image incorporating the chosen symbolism, simple enough to engrave on witch jewels and to visualize clearly in meditation.

Coven Hierarchy

Witch covens, like most secret magickal societies, have organized themselves into hierarchies since the earliest times. The policy of the group is directed by one or more leaders, traditionally held to be wiser, stronger, or simply more experienced than the rest. A leader holds their position until it is either successfully challenged or handed on to a successor.

The Three Leaders

There may be as many as three leaders:

  1. The Magister / High Priest: the male leader, representing masculine power. Also titled: Cernunnos, Dumus, Puck, Hu, Barabbas, Mamilion, Dianus / Janus, Janicot, The Devil (meaning "little god," from early Aryan div, "holy" or "shining"), Lucifer ("the light bearer"), Simon, Herne, Gogmagog, Andros, Adonai / Adonis, Sabaoth, Baphomet.
  2. The Lady / High Priestess: the female leader, representing feminine power. Also titled: Andred, Bensozia, Nocticula, Rhiannon, Arrianrhod, Herodias / Aradia, Habondia / Dame Habonde, Holda / Hulda, Morgan / Morrigan, Brigid / Bride, Astarte / Ishtar, The Virgin / Maiden (Persephone).
  3. The Summoner / Officer / Executor: the second male, acting as the magister's lieutenant and go-between. He handles mundane coven functions: membership, dues, timing and location of Sabbats, what to wear and what to bring. He may lead the coven in the magister's absence. Traditionally wore all black; also titled "the Man in Black." In medieval France sometimes dressed in green and called Verdelet. His badge of office was a blackthorn staff, also called "Black Rod."

The relative authority of the Lady versus the Magister varies by tradition. In knowledge-and-power covens, the lady holds little executive authority and may function as a seer under the magister's direction. In goddess-oriented covens, the high priestess leads, and the high priest is her consort.

Dress and Regalia

The magister may wear furs, a robe, or nothing at all. On his head he may wear a traditional shamanic horned helmet, a full animal-head mask representing a coven totem (goat, ram, horse, cat, or other), or a closed metal helmet (hence the old epithet "Old Brazen Nose"). During Sabbats, his headpiece bears a short candle at the center, lit during proceedings, symbolizing his role as Lord of the Sun, Lucifer the light bearer.

The high priestess may similarly be robed or unrobed. Robe colors vary: white is most common, but black, green, red, or blue have all been used. On her forehead she may bind a silver lunar crescent, horns upward, or wear her hair flowing free. During Sabbat dances she may wear an illuminated coronet of candles. She always wears her full witch jewels, including the mandatory necklace.

Coven members may bring their own robes or work nude. A uniform cowled black robe or tabard is considered ideal for collective working. All members should wear witch jewels and bring their athames and wands. In earlier times, gentry brought swords and peasants brought pitchforks; the wand was disguised as a broomstick for concealment.

On Sacrifice

The notion that coven leaders were once periodically killed as a magickal sacrifice is likely more connected with beliefs fostered by established priesthoods, such as the Druids, than with actual witch coven practice. The concept of guilt, scapegoats, and atonement is absent from witchcraft.

The only rituals currently involving anything of this nature are cakes and wine and libations. The occasional use of a minute quantity of blood in certain operations is not understood as appeasement but as a means of conveying a specific type of magickal energy held to reside in the blood. Many modern witches prefer the white of an egg as a substitute.

The Bed as Altar

In fertility magick, the conjugal bed is not merely furniture, it is a primary sacred space, treated as one would any ritual altar. It can be spiritually cleansed, adorned with meaningful objects, hung with charms and talismans, and consciously demarcated as an enchanted space. Spells that incorporate the bed work by suffusing the most intimate space in the home with fertility energy, so that rest and lovemaking both occur within an already-charged field of intention.

Magick's Most Primordial Subject

Of all the purposes to which magick has ever been turned, wealth, luck, love, healing, power, none is older or more intrinsic than fertility. The earliest known religious traditions were not preoccupied with death but with generation: with the mysteries of birth, life, and the creative force that perpetuates both. Their sacred images were not skulls or tombs but the human genitals, rendered in clay, carved into stone, worn close to the body.

Language preserves the trace of this. The word venerate shares its root with Venus, venerable, and venereal, all branching from the same ancient source, a concept encompassing love, desire, and the sacred power of generation.

Fertility and Magick Are the Same Force

The kinship runs deeper than metaphor. Magick, at its core, attempts to create something that did not previously exist, to bring the possible into the actual. This is precisely what generation does. It is no coincidence that the spirits most intimately involved with magick are the same ones governing human reproductive capacity: Hekate, Artemis, Yemaya, Baba Yaga, Freya, Oshun, Áine, and many others all hold dominion over both.

Magickal tools carry this association as well. Mortars and pestles, sieves, cauldrons, broomsticks, wands, and staffs are simultaneously fertility symbols. Their power is drawn, at least in part, from their resonance with the generative act. To some extent the phrase sex magick is redundant: the sexual act is inherently magickal. Like any magickal working, it can be performed well or badly, with intention or without, honored or profaned. Violence and coercion destroy its sacred dimension entirely.

Reproductive Control, Not Just Conception

Fertility magick is not simply about having children. The operative concept is control over one's own reproductive capacity, the power to conceive when and if one chooses, and equally, to prevent conception when one does not. The earliest magickal systems were also medical systems; no sharp line divided the two. Holistic traditions gave as much attention to botanicals that prevent or end pregnancy as to those that encourage it. Many of the most revered witch-spirits, Hekate, Kybele, Artemis, Baba Yaga, were master herbalists whose knowledge of plants served both ends.

Fertility magick also extends beyond literal conception. The same generative force that creates life also creates art, music, writing, and all other forms of making. These spells may be adapted freely to stimulate creative fertility of any kind.

Fertility as Latent Capacity

Fertility is not a thing one either has or lacks, it is a capacity that exists to be drawn upon when desired. In this sense it closely resembles one's capacity for magick itself: one need not cast a spell every day, but the power should be available when called upon. Whether one intends to conceive or never to conceive, the aim of fertility magick is to keep that capacity intact, available, and under one's own authority.

A Note on Magick and Conception

Fertility magick works in concert with, not in place of, the physical act of conception. No working, however well-crafted or potently supplied, can substitute for well-timed sex. These spells are aids, amplifiers, and aligners, not replacements.

Botanicals of Fertility

Many fertility-boosting plants announce their power through visible signs: a resemblance to human genitalia, a close affiliation with the moon, or seeds produced in such extravagant quantity that abundance seems to be their nature. Botanicals that fall into one or more of these categories include assorted snake roots, black-eyed peas, corn, figs, jasmine, lilies, lotuses, melons, moonflowers, mugwort, assorted nuts, olives, pomegranates, poppies, pumpkins, roses, and wheat.

Candle Magick for Fertility

Candlelight is a natural companion to fertility workings. Red candles are the most common choice, though figure candles carry particular resonance: a single human figure representing the spell-caster, or a conjoined male-and-female figure candle. Other potent forms include red cat candles, red witch candles, snake candles, and candles cast in the shape of hearts or genitalia. Each of these shapes carries symbolic weight that amplifies the central intention.

Botanical Safety Warning

The boundaries between fertility magick and traditional botanical medicine are especially fluid and require particular care. Many botanicals used to encourage conception in cases of serious infertility are unsafe during pregnancy itself, particularly in the early weeks. Topical application, in baths or massage oils, can be as potent as or more potent than internal use. As a general rule, essential oils should be avoided during pregnancy, especially in the first trimester. Choose spells and botanicals carefully and consult relevant safety resources before working with any plant material in a reproductive context.

Transformation and the Phoenix

When humans discovered fire and learned how to use it, their lives were transformed. Thus the fire element is associated with transformation. Think of the mythical phoenix rising from the flames, a symbol of fiery transformation. If you seek to transform something in your life, whether a relationship, career path, or health condition, tap into fire's dynamic power.

Fire's Volatile Nature

Fire energy moves rapidly and is volatile and unpredictable. Think of how a wildfire can rage out of control or how lightning bursts in the sky. Draw on fire when you want to kick your spell's power up a notch or see rapid results.

Fire Applications:

  • Banish fear
  • See the future
  • Purification spells and rituals
  • Amplify spell power
  • Rapid transformation

Fire Personalities

People who have a lot of fire energy in their makeup tend to be self-confident, passionate, impulsive, outgoing, vigorous, and courageous individuals. Fire conveys inspiration, enthusiasm, vitality, and daring.

Fire in Spell-casting

Fire is the most self-willed of the elements, answering to no one and resisting every attempt at containment. It can heal, charge, scrub clean, and refine. It is the great transformer, and it demands respect above all else. While any element can turn dangerous (floods, mudslides, tornadoes), fire is typically the most hazardous. No amount of spiritual focus replaces common sense fire safety. Never assume that ritual context makes open flame risk free. Stay alert.

Fire is a masculine, yang force. Candle magick is its most popular expression, but magickal bonfires and oil lamps serve the same purpose. Magick mirrors sometimes harness the raw, shape shifting force of flame, creative and destructive in equal measure.

Capnomancy

Capnomancy receives its oracle from images perceived in the smoke of large ritual fires and bonfires. Enhance its divinatory power by burning herbs associated with psychic vision: mugwort, wormwood, Syrian rue, and diviner's sage.

Tephramancy

Tephramancy reads the ashes, cinders, and soot left behind after a fire has gone out. The more sacred the fire, the greater weight the information carries. Once hearth fires or ritual bonfires have cooled, examine the ash for letters, words, or shapes emerging from the remains. No formulated question is necessary; the practice is one of open reception rather than directed inquiry.

Fire in Myth and Landscape

"Just as a candle cannot burn without fire, men cannot live without a spiritual life."
The Buddha

The Shape of Fire

More than any of the other three elements, fire holds both the power to create and the power to destroy. Its symbol is the upright triangle, and the plainest thing humans have built in that shape is the pyramid, whose very name comes from the Greek word for fire. In the natural world its clearest form is the Holy Mountain, the mound of earth that rose up out of the primal waters.

Spirit and Eternal Life

Fire also stands for the spirit and for life itself. We talk of the spark of life as though it were a kind of flame. The eternal flames kept in temples and churches of every denomination, like the Olympic torch, stand for life that never ends. In the Acts of the Apostles the Holy Spirit descends among Christ's disciples as "tongues like flames of fire," and the phoenix, burning itself to nothing, is born again out of the very same fire.

The Purifying Flame

As a cleansing force, fire is the favored way of laying the body to rest in many religions. The flames and smoke carry the spirit upward toward the Heavens while purifying the body through destruction, much as they do for the phoenix. For the same reason fire served as a means of sacrifice, a fitting way to make an offering to the gods. The ashes left once the flames have finished their work carry their own meaning, marking our return to the dust from which the material body is made. As vibhuti, the ash of cow dung burned in the sacred fire, or homa, it is used to mark tilaka, sacred signs of devotion, onto the foreheads and bodies of Hindu ascetics, showing that they have turned away from the lures of the material world toward the spiritual. The Celts put the purifying power of fire to work at Beltane on the first of May, when cattle were driven between two great bonfires in the hope of warding off disease. Later the Great Fire of London, even as it razed much of the city, was held to have burned away the horrors of the plague. We may be baptized in water, yet we also speak of a baptism of fire, a swift and testing ordeal of initiation that leads to enlightenment once its purification is done. In Sanskrit the words for pure and for fire are one and the same.

Fire and Water

A Fulani saying captures the bond between the two elements neatly:

"Fire comes from Heaven, because it goes up. Water comes from Earth, because it comes down as rain."

Where water can lie as still and clear as a mirror, the nature of fire is ceaseless movement, never pausing for a moment until its fuel is spent.

Passion and the Spark

Fire is bound up closely with passion and sexual energy. When people first learned to kindle it, they did so by rubbing two things together with an up-and-down motion whose friction struck the first spark, and the sexual symbolism of the act is hard to miss. Flames raised this way were seen as either demonic or divine, and an old belief held that fire was somehow gestated within the genitals of a sorceress. The erect phallus, too, stands as a symbol of fire.
